speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been a long, drawn-out debate. The issues are well known to the House, to the media and across the country, and I am afraid that as far as members of this parliament are concerned convictions have hardened and people have already made up their minds.
The reason I am boring the House today with a short contribution to this debate is simply that I have not spoken on the matter yet in this chamber. Frankly, I feel somewhat uncomfortable for that reason since, as usual, my own views and experiences do not parallel those of anyone else in the House. I feel I have a duty to indicate those views and experiences in the course of this debate, especially so that my constituents may be able to judge them. As a matter of fact, I think we all have a duty and a responsibility as elected representatives to voice the opinions, desires and needs of our own constituents not only on this issue but on other issues that come before us. I ask you rhetorically, if I may, Mr. Speaker: Why are we all here if it is not to represent the views of our constituents? I ask a further question: Is there anybody here who believes he has been elected to come here because, in the opinion of his constituents, he knows better than they what is good for them?
I think there can be no doubt whatever respecting the feelings and opinions of by far the larger number of people in this country on the general issue of capital punishment. A great number of public opinion polls have been taken on the subject, some of them scientific, others unscientific. I have yet to see one of them which indicated there was a majority of opinion in favour of the abolition of capital punishment in this country. I have seen a great number of these polls and the number of citizens expressing a desire to retain capital punishment for the crime of wanton, premeditated murder ranges from a low of 60 per cent to a high of more than 90 per cent. I believe that especially on an emotional issue such as this the opinions, the sensibilities, the conscience of the average citizen are every bit as reliable as those of any member of parliament, and that we
in this House have a responsibility to conform to the clearly expressed wishes of those who elected us.
Because of the intervention of the recess may I take a moment to remind hon. members of what we are discussing. I point out to hon. members that prior to the Criminal Code 1967 Amendment Act a planned and deliberate capital murder in this country was punishable by death, but since 1967 the killing of police officers and prison authorities acting in the course of their duties have been the only murder offences punishable by death under the law. We have gone through the period of the so-called five-year moratorium.

speechtext:
What some people will do to get extra applause, Mr. Speaker! In any event, I was indicating that over the last five years the killing of police officers and prison authorities acting within the course of their duties have been the only murder offences punishable by death under our law. This, as I said, was the period of the so-called five-year moratorium. But under the bill we now have before us, the amendment we have just finished discussing as well as the amendment we are discussing now, the issue to be decided by us, all of us, is whether that moratorium should be continued, whether offences calling for capital punishment should be widened, or the further alternative of whether we go back to the pre-1967 state of our law.
Whether we go back to the pre-1967 state of the law or not, for me this debate and the time we have all devoted to it has had a real air of futility and frustration about it. I say that because, even though we know what the law is, since 1967 no police killers and no prison guard killers have been executed in this country despite the fact that in the four years from 1967 through to 1970 16 policemen in this country were murdered in the course of their duties. All of the killers, when convicted of capital murder, had their penalties commuted by the cabinet under the procedure known as the royal prerogative of mercy.
The royal prerogative of mercy is a further appeal that is built into our system under which, after all the trial and appeal procedures in the courts are completed, the cabinet discusses whether or not the penalty should be carried out. I feel that the royal prerogative is a protective, sensible

and needed provision in our legal system in case there is new evidence or other factors that indicate a miscarriage of judgment at the trial and/or the appeal processes of our court system, or some other honest doubt has been created about the guilt of the accused. But I say to you, Sir, that this procedure was never designed to subvert the law. It was never designed to subvert the opinion of parliament and the people. It was never designed to undermine the morale of our law enforcement agencies or the processes of our judicial system. Yet under successive governments, not just this one but successive governments, the law of this country has not been upheld; commutation of these death penalties has been automatic and has been expected.
I suspect that despite this debate today, what has gone on before and what will follow, and no matter what the decision of parliament is, no matter what people's opinions may be and no matter what the laws says, under this government we will continue to have the death penalty commuted. Therefore this debate is frustrating and futile because it will have no realistic effect whatsoever. Nevertheless, there is a bill before us. It was drafted by the government, approved by cabinet and is supported unanimously by the ministry. We are now debating it and will vote on it as if it could change the situation.
The purpose of the amendment we have just finished discussing, introduced by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin), calls for the institution of the death penalty where death results from capital murder committed during the course of a rape. If the hon. lady were in the House I would say to her that I certainly intend to support her amendment. My own amendment deals with two matters. It deals with a murder, a killing, a death as a direct result of an act of air piracy or, as we familiarly call it, hijacking. Second, it provides that the death penalty will be instituted where a second conviction for murder occurs. My intention obviously is to vote for my own amendment as it is to vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert.
I hope the hon. lady will not mind if I tell her that even if her amendment is carried and even if my own amendment is carried I intend to vote against third reading of the bill. My logic or the lack of it, as some may claim, is simply this. I do not believe that the bill before us is complete. Obviously, this is one of the reasons why I introduced an amendment. I believe we should go back to the pre-1967 law where for all cases of capital murder the death penalty is instituted. In the case of the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert and my own amendment, if the bill is defeated on third reading, we go back to the pre-1967 law which includes the offences that are before us today and, of course, a great many other offences. It will not include air piracy or hijacking, of course, but I hope that is something the House can clear up in another manner after third reading. However, in respect of the rape provision and the double murder provision, obviously the pre-1967 law will include both of these offences and others.
May I now speak for a moment on the question of air piracy or hijacking. I wish to quote some statistics that have not been quoted in the House before because the matter was not before us. Hon. members may be surprised

to learn that the first recorded attempt, and a successful attempt at that, to hijack took place in 1933. According to the Lloyd's list, between 1933 and 1968 there were in all 100 international attempts to hijack aircraft in the world. All of those attempts were successful.
In 1967 the problem suddenly worsened. It accelerated drastically. All governments, airlines and airports began improving security. In 1969 there were 86 recorded attempts in the world in respect of the hijacking of planes of scheduled airlines. In 1970 there were 80 recorded attempts, 62 in 1971 and 60 in 1972. In actual fact, the number of recorded attempts to hijack in the world has declined very slowly, but I wish to point out to the House that as time went on hijackings became much more dangerous, violent and difficult.
Up to the middle of August there have been this year seven internationally recorded attempts to hijack. These statistics show that while the number of acts or attempts at air piracy is decreasing, the property damage, the number of aircraft destroyed and the number of persons killed or injured are increasing quite rapidly. In the period 1968-71, there were 12 passengers or crew members and 18 hijackers killed. An additional 71 people were injured. In 1972 alone there were 13 passengers or crew members and 22 hijackers killed. The number of fatalities in 1972 was more than the combined total of the previous four years. In 1972, 29 other people were injured as the result of hijacking attempts.
The figures for this year are incomplete and therefore I cannot give them. In May, 1973, a Russian Aeroflot TU-104 was hijacked over southern Siberia. The aircraft crashed, presumably killing all aboard, after a gunfight between the hijacker and an armed guard. The number of casualties has never been announced by the U.S.S.R.
The statistics and the trend of the figures are there. This is a serious problem. It is getting more serious. Strong, deterrent action is needed because with the trend toward larger aeroplanes and more air miles covered each year there is potential danger to a growing number of innocent people who use the airlines of this country and the world.
To date, Canada has been remarkably free from hijackings with only a few attempts, but the situation can change. Hijacking is an international offence or, if not, it should be, and we in this country are in danger of these matters flopping over or slopping over into our jurisdiction. If the House does decide that the death penalty is required, I think that strong deterrent action and statutory law are necessary.
May I now move on to the other thrust of my amendment, namely, that in the case of a second conviction for capital murder, the death penalty should apply. I think this is obvious and I do not intend to speak long on it. Certainly our penal and police records show that some in this country who have committed murder have done so more than once. Many have done it more than twice. For example, we all got rather excited just last May when there was an escape from the Laval Correctional Development Centre. One of the persons who escaped at that time and who had broken out twice from an institution was described by the minister at that time as the meanest and toughest type of inmate. That escapee was a confessed double murderer.

Surely there can be no doubt about a repeater. If the death penalty is to remain for anyone surely there should be no doubt that on a second conviction the ultimate penalty should be applied. I say that because surely it is a wrong toward our fellow man and society in general to allow a dangerous undesirable criminal to remain in that society with the probability of causing further harm. This is the basis of my thinking in respect of the whole issue of capital punishment. When the Solicitor General, as he so often has in the House during this debate and in committee and through the media and elsewhere, asks how can we possibly help the victim by executing the offender, my answer to him is simply this: Mr. Solicitor General, you are on the wrong tack completely. When a man or woman has been killed no one can possibly help them. What we should be worried about is the protection in the future of other innocents.
Let me give you my own historical background, Mr. Speaker, in respect of this whole question, because at one time I was an abolitionist. I felt and still feel that hanging is a repugnant act. I still feel that the execution of my fellow man is a terrifying admission of our own failure. Nevertheless, at one time I had some responsibility for the safety and public security of our citizens. At that time I must admit to you, Sir, I went through a real evolution in my mental processes and attitude toward the whole question. I am now a retentionist in respect of capital punishment.

May I take the time of the House merely to say to you, Sir, that the final element in my conversion took place in the spring of 1971 as a result of what we now call the Kingston riot and the subsequent trial of 13 inmates of Kingston, more familiarly known in the legal profession in this province as the infamous Kingston 13. Let me take you back to the evening of Friday, April 18, 1971, at Kingston penitentiary, Kingston, Ontario. At approximately 8.30 p.m. on that evening the ringleaders, a portion of the inmates of that institution, overpowered their guards and took over the institution. For three days within that federal institution there was utter chaos, utter confusion and absolute rampage. During the first two days savage beatings took place and indescribable acts of sadism and bestiality. Some of these matters have never been made public.
On the second night, Saturday night, the segregated prisoners from the first floor of the institution were taken from that floor into the middle of the dome of Kingston penitentiary. Kingston penitentiary, for the information of members, generally speaking is built in the form of a cross with a wing extending out on either side. In the centre of this cross is the area called the dome which extends from the first floor to the ceiling. You can look into the dome area down on to the floor below. The segregated prisoners, what the inmates call the finks, the diddlers and the stoolies, were gathered together by the ringleaders. They were taken to the main floor. The area is about 50 feet across. In the centre of that well is a circular radiator. Fourteen of the inmates were dragged to this radiator ostensibly to be used as a bargaining lever in respect of

the whole riot. They were tied facing inward on steel chairs and then all of the chairs were chained together.
At this time the whole institution was controlled by and in the power of the ringleaders. All of the inmates of the institution were then called by the ringleaders to come out on to the balconies to watch the show that was about to take place. At about 2.00 a.m. on Sunday the show started. I do not intend to indicate to you, Sir, all of the details of what took place. I merely say that it started by the beating of these 14 men with steel locking bars taken from the doors which lock the cells in the penitentiary itself. As the turn of each of these 14 poor individuals came about the ringleaders would call out to the assembled crowd, "Do you like this guy?" Invariably, because of the nature of the offence for which that person was in custody, the answer was a resounding "no".
In almost every case as the ringleaders went about the first thing that happened was that the kneecaps of the individuals were smashed. That was just the beginning. Their noses were then smashed. Later indescribable acts took place with straight razors and instruments such as that. That went on for four hours. It was all over by five o'clock. Most of the 14 inmates were terribly lacerated and horribly mutilated. Some of them will never move again under their own power. It is a miracle that only two died, one almost immediately and the other several days later as a result of his injuries. These two people were Ensor and Robert. They had cranial injuries. Others were maimed. Thirteen inmates were charged, all of whom were between the age of 18 and 39.
In the ensuing investigations that took place at Kingston there were very great difficulties in identification. Some of the people who came forward to identify those who took part in these acts are still in security and solitary confinement today because the Solicitor General and his officials, quite rightly, cannot allow these people to intermix with the rest of the prison population for fear of what would happen to them. The difficulties of identification were immense. All prisoners were interrogated and all the prisoners who were charged, the Kingston 13, were people who were in Kingston as a result of rape charges, robbery with violence charges, gross indecency charges as well as other offences. One of the 13 had previously been convicted of manslaughter. Two of the 13 had previously been convicted of murder but had had their sentences commuted.
The purpose of bringing these matters forward is to indicate the mentality of a small portion, a very infinitesimal minority, of the people of this country. There are people whose mentality is such as I have just described. They are not safe, whether they are in prison or outside of prison. As a matter of fact, one of these people has since escaped from Mi'lhaven. I believe there are some members of the prison population of this country whom it is not possible to rehabilitate. They can be identified by medical tests and they are known to the counselling staff. They have been given every psychiatric and sociological test in our prisons, and our prison authorities know who these people are.

I spoke to one very well known member of the Ontario legal profession after a trial. My job was to supervise legal aid at the time to ensure that prisoners had access to it. I asked him what he thought about his client and he said: "Al, that man was pure brute". Another well known counsel came to me after the trial and indicated that his client was all animal. I simply say that when there is such a prisoner, the other prisoners and even the prison staff live in perpetual fear for their lives and safety. Some of these people are in solitary confinement. They are isolated from the rest of the prison population not for purposes of punishment or for the purpose of rehabilitation, not for revenge or retribution, but solely and simply for the purpose of protecting everyone else in the prison.
There are people in our prisons today, some of whom were involved in the Kingston riot, whose only seeming purpose in life is to kill others. One Kingston guard said to me that one of those individuals who was involved in the Kingston riot would obviously kill anyone who came within three feet of him. If anyone came within striking distance of him, that prisoner would strike. As long as there are such people alive today, whether they are in prison or outside of it, there is a real danger that other persons, in some cases innocent persons, will be in danger because of the mentality of that individual.
I say to you, Sir, forget the philosophical discussions in which we have all been engaged in the House on whether capital punishment is or is not a deterrent. Forget these claims about how hanging brutalizes our society. If you want, even forget the horrifying execution practices that still exist in this country. Forget some of the statistics that have been fed to us ad nauseam about the increase in violence and murder in this country. I ask you, Sir, and hon. members to think for just a moment of the future and of the innocent people who can still be killed, tragically maimed or injured by people who have a mentality such as I have described. There will be people who will be brutally killed in the future if people like this are left alive today. They constitute, obviously, an infinitesimal minority, but if we do not retain the death penalty for these people I think we will be abrogating our responsibility so far as the future is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the amendments placed before us this morning I wish to go on record now as saying that unfortunately I will not be in the House this evening at 10.45 to vote. I have voted for the bill in the past, but there will be one less vote this evening. However, I am about to do something that six months ago I would not have thought possible. I intend to change my vote on third reading of Bill C-2. In so doing, I wish to point out with every ounce of energy I possess that I have not changed my principles. First, last and always, I deplore the taking of the life of a human being in any way, shape or form. I cannot, and will not, change this basic principle and cannot envisage any situation which would alter my determination. Coming to the decision to change my vote, however, has been a long and painful process, and I intend to delve into that process briefly to justify this action which is so unfamiliar to me.
When the bill was introduced I studied it very carefully, fully realizing all its shortcomings. I realized that similar legislation had been in effect for five years, that it had not been followed, to the everlasting discredit of the government composed in part of those opposite me-had it been followed, there would perhaps have been a real analysis of the worth of such legislation-that the bill continued discrimination between classes of people, giving protection to those who carry firearms and none to those who do not, that it did not provide the public with protection from disturbed persons with a tendency to kill, and that it did not protect the public from the abuses of the Parole Act or change it in any way. I was fully aware of all these things, and I know the feelings of my constituents. I too listened to the people in my riding and talked to them about this sort of thing.
With all this in mind, I still felt I had to support the bill at second reading for two main reasons, both of which support my initial, basic principle. I believed, first, that it was the best legislation we would get from this weak government. Second, it was my understanding that legislative safeguards would be introduced which would protect the public and put at ease the minds of ordinary men and women who read time after time of atrocities committed by parolees, of the hotel-like atmosphere of our penal institutions, of repeated leaves, and of the pampering of convicted persons, all without any visible improvement in the crime rate or the penal system. So I voted for the government bill. I did so, content that some of the men and women from both sides of the House whose opinions I respect most highly voted as I did. I did so asking for the understanding of my constituents, both those who supported as well as those who opposed my stand. I did so knowing how emotional the subject was and yet how basically unimportant the bill is at this time of frightening inflation and unemployment, at a time when amongst our native peoples more persons are in danger of death from starvation, under nourishment and neglect than from violence.
I did not speak on the subject prior to the second reading of the bill. I could have and perhaps have added a
Criminal Code
tiny bit to the debate. The nonsense with regard to a referendum could, I feel, be shot down easily. The weight of evidence, to a reasoning person, indicates that capital punishment is not a deterrent. I could have used the Bible as a reference manual, as both sides have done in their presentations. I could have but I did not because I felt that the time being taken could be put to a better purpose having regard to the vital necessity of discussion and legislation on economic matters. I do not intend to dwell on the amendments, although support of the motion of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) and the motion of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) would make as much sense to me as the two classes of people named in the bill as it now stands. I could, but for that reason I am not going to do so.
Given all the foregoing, Mr. Speaker, 1 am now prepared to change my vote, for three reasons. The prime reason, the overwhelming compulsion to go contrary to my initial instincts and vote against the bill, is that the fumbling and bumbling of the government have not only not produced any safeguards for the public but have allowed the continuation of practices which have produced the intolerable situations that are so evident today. We still find totally unrehabilitated criminals on the loose, either with the blessing of and at times financed by the government, or having escaped because of incredibly inept administration of our penal institutions.
There are still laws on the books that allow a man to kill two teenagers and get off with only a fine of $125, excused simply because he was intoxicated and driving a motor vehicle. If this man had soberly stopped his car and bludgeoned them to death his fate would have been far different. To me this does not seem to be any safeguard for the public. In short, instead of taking into consideration the obvious and frequently voiced requests of the majority of Canadians, the government has gone blindly and blithely on its way. It has not taken a single, serious, considered step toward penal reform that will either protect the public or, for that matter, benefit those within the institutions.
Second, in voting against this bill I am content in my own mind that I am not jeopardizing the life of anyone. Since the cabinet in defiance of its own legislation has not seen fit to carry out the death penalty, even when called for under the experimental act of the last five years, I see no imminent possibility of a reversal of its attitude. How much easier it would have been for those of us who favour abolition of the death penalty if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet had followed the act, because then we would have had something on which to base our decision instead of the farce we have had up to now.
Finally, and I dislike intensely using this argument, I feel that the bungling, inefficient handling of this legislation in every phase does not deserve support. That argument alone would not change my mind when the life of anyone, even of a convicted murderer, was at stake. But since, as I have said, I see no danger, it must be considered. 1 cannot believe that the minister was so naive as to allow the debate to go on as long as it did without giving any indication of his intention to alter the bill drastically in committee if there had not been some intention to deceive not only members of the House but the public at

large. If the minister has no better appreciation of the problems of our penal system, of the mood of the country, or even of the rules of parliament than to make such a stupid, blundering attempt, his legislation does not deserve my support.
As I said at the beginning my principles have not changed. I still believe strongly in the futility of taking any life. In voting against the legislation I do so in the anticipation that, hopefully, with a good deal more com-monsense and perhaps with an entirely new minister we may have legislation presented that will clean up this sorry mess. Hopefully we will have legislation that will provide for the people of Canada the safeguards that they expect and deserve, that will provide for those within our institutions a rehabilitation process that must surely be less costly than our present methods of incarceration, that will provide for the humane segregation of incorrigibles in institutions, thus not allowing either escapes or riots such as we have experienced in the last few years.
My family, my friends and constituents are aware of the difficulty I have had in making this decision and, while they may have tried, my colleagues have in no way influenced my change of heart. I have made my decision freely and hopefully in expectation of a new approach to this very difficult problem.

Mr. Speaker, we are now considering the amendment of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) on capital punishment.
Before the adjournment I had the opportunity to state my views to the House. Since then, we have got acquainted with those entertained here and there in Canada. As the mover said a while ago: Canadians in general object to the abolition of capital punishment. There are some exceptions. We hear sometimes that we do not have the right to hang someone in revenge. I think that we must upheld the principle of-

speechtext:
The abortionists, as mentioned by the member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), have the right to do so, but to punish a gangster or kill him if he has committed a murder, this is not allowed.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the principle is not based on revenge and I would be sorry if it were. It is not an emotional issue either but a matter of protecting the community. If, for example, an individual has a piece of land which is dangerous, he is compelled to set up a fence. For example, at my place in Hull I have a swimming pool. The law requires me to put a fence around my swimming pool so that young children for instance might not fall in it and drown. That is altogether normal and in order. And so capital punishment, in my view, is precisely a fence which sometimes keeps people from committing deeds that they would not commit if there were a barrier, a fence. In my
[Mr. Ellis.)
view, capital punishment is the barrier which invites a criminal to refrain from committing murder. It is especially in that spirit that we oppose the abolition of capital punishment. We claim that the amendments now before us are not serious enough to enable us to adequately protect society.
I have received in the mail two letters and one telegram in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. One telegram from Ottawa, for instance, was sent to me by a Mr. Rodrigue Tremblay who sends me his impressions.
Mr. Caouette in regard to your meeting in Ottawa since your last three days relative to the death penalty for prisoners accused of murder you are hereby advised that I myself and my community-

I do not know what community he wants to refer to.
[ English]
-shall fight against you because five years ago it was taken off for a good psychological purpose. I myself and other people of my community are telling you not to exercise your powers so much and keep on salesman for selling cars. Yours truly, Roderick Tremblay.

Mr. Speaker, if people in favour of capital punishment or its abolition all reason like that I think it is a rather faulty line of reasoning. On the other hand, the two other letters I have here express views against capital punishment on religious grounds: Thou shall not kill, etc. But when I consider the truly serious mail I receive from various points in Canada I see that some people are in favour of capital punishment. For example, I have here a letter from Miss Irene Bird of Regina. That person is all in favour of retaining capital punishment. Somebody sent me a newspaper clipping from the Quebec L'Action of July 24, 1973, where the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) is reported as saying in the House, on television and elsewhere, and I quote:
"How in God's name do we pretend to help the stricken family by killing another person".
That is a most nonsensical line of reasoning. We hear things like that but where is the seriousness in them?
The minister received a letter from a lawyer who is certainly as important as he is. Incidentally, I will tell the Solicitor General that there are Liberal members seated behind him or on his side who do not share his views at all. They found deplorable the approach he took with respect to capital punishment and the amendments before us.
I have here a letter from a rather influential lawyer in Montreal, Mr. K. H. Brown, Q.C. For the information of the Solicitor General, I will quote it. And that letter is dated September 25. So it is rather recent.

-I very much appreciated your thoughtful letter of July 26, 1973, answering mine of July 24 with which I had sent you a copy of my brief dated June 11, 1973 to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
That brief was in fact a retitled version of a memorandum dated March 9, 1973, which I had sent to a number of members-
October 18, 1973



I am not the only one who received this letter. Some Montreal members have also received a copy.

-from whom (notably Mr. Woolliams and Mr. Nielsen)-

-two Progressive Conservatives have also received it. [English]
I had received appreciative replies. More formal replies were received from several other Conservatives, and some Liberal members to whom I had sent copies of the memorandum because they had spoken in the House in favour of capital punishment.

As I said, this letter has not been written by a nobody, but by a lawyer, an experienced man from a very important law office which employs at least twenty lawyers, Lafleur et Brown, in Montreal. The Solicitor General is certainly not aware of that.

I now note that the matter is to receive top priority when parliament reconvenes on October 15 and, since you and those to whom I am sending copies of this letter are clearly interested in the matter to the point of taking positive action, I venture to suggest that, apart from the obvious course of persuading as many members as possible, regardless of party, to vote against the bill, these members (or some of them) might consider advancing the arguments which I am mentioning below, which I have not seen pressed very hard so far.
I realize that Madame Morin's two amendments are still under debate, and of course they are desirable as far as they go, but I still think that the bill itself should be relentlessly attacked, and defeated if possible.
[ Translation]
This is what we are going to help to do, that is defeat this bill.
[ English]
I would first refer to Mr. Allmand's constant theme, last expressed I think in the House of Commons on July 23, 1973 (see Hansard of that date, page 5902) as follows:
How in God's name do we help the victim or help the family by hanging the murderer? If any hon. member ... can show me we can help the victim or the family of the murdered person by hanging somebody, I would be happy and willing to change my position.
[ Translation]
I for one would feel uneasy to stay on such a position. [English]
It seems to me that the best attack here would be to challenge Mr. Allmand, directly, to produce one single instance of anybody ever having said that killing a live man could help a dead one or his family. If he cannot (and of course he cannot because obviously nobody ever said anything so silly), it might be suggested that he stop talking as though anyone had ever said such a thing, and trying to make a case for himself by demolishing a non-existent argument.

I repeat, these are empty arguments.

That line of attack would of course lead directly into the argument about deterrence, and the usual figures, criminologists' reports, etc., would no doubt be invoked by Mr. Allmand.
Criminal Code
At this juncture it might be helpful to draw an analogy based upon something which every member of parliament must have experienced in his own personal life. Often it is more useful to bring the matter "close to home" in this way than to debate on a higher but not necessarily more theoretical level.
It could first be pointed out that deterrence is obviously almost entirely a subjective area in which actual proof is next to impossible to obtain (though I did point to specific, proven cases in my brief) because people are simply not going to come forward and say "I was deterred from committing murder".
That much having been pointed out, it becomes evident that the figures, if they prove anything, can only prove that there does exist a hard core class of criminals who cannot be deterred by the death penalty or by anything else.
This is where the analogy might be brought in and I suggest that members be invited to cast their minds back to their school days, as I have done, and I think my experience was typical.
I was in a class of say 30 boys. Punishment for misconduct ranged from the strap as a maximum, down through detention after normal school hours for various periods, deprivation of certain privileges, etc.
Now in that class of 30 there always was a hard core of, say, two or three who were not deterred by the strap or anything else, but surely that would not have been a reason for eliminating it as an effective deterrent for the other 27 or 28 in the class, which it certainly was.
I think that the analogy is complete but in any case I submit it for whatever it may be worth.
As I said before, it is my hope that your evident interest, and that of the gentlemen to whom I am sending copies of this letter, in this matter may make it possible for you to think up some way of making a co-ordinated, organized attack on the bill by members, regardless of their party affiliations, who will have fortified themselves by searching out all possible sources of information and arguments beforehand. I am certain that a fully organized attack is of critical importance because there is certainly a powerful organization supporting the bill.
If my brief to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, or this letter, or any other material which I can furnish, will be of any help, please let me know. Copies of the brief are of course available from the secretary of committees of the House, and if you would like any further copies of this letter you can telephone me or my secretary "collect" and the copies will be forwarded at once.
Yours sincerely,
K. H. Brown, Q.C.
Copies of this letter were sent to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen).
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, this letter comes from a Montreal legal firm. I have received, from Montreal also, a letter written by Mr. Bouthillier, which ends as follows:
I believe that it was necessary to give these arguments in order to shed more light on the study of the bill which will be brought before the House of Commons and which will probably have serious consequences for the welfare of the Canadian citizens.
It seems necessary to maintain capital punishment in order not to abolish the equal rights of all citizens to life and death, especially since the extenuating circumstances stipulated in the Criminal Code have already reduced to a minimum the number of executions.
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that the law must be amended so as to eliminate risks and uncertainties. When there is any doubt as to the guilt of a murderer, he should be given the benefit of the doubt. However, if there is no question

October 18, 1973
Criminal Code
concerning his guilt, if the case is absolutely clear, accurate and f roven, then society should be protected against criminals.
In fact, certain countries, like England, who had abolished the death penalty a few years ago, are seriously considering re-establishing it. I have right here a newspaper article stating the position taken recently by the State of California. I quote:

California returns to capital punishment on a limited basis. [Translation]
Some countries will resort again to capital punishment. In Canada, it is right to say that "for the sake of humanitarianism", "for the sake of the individual" the one who killed, even if he were fully conscious of the seriousness of his act, he should not be sentenced to hang.
Mr. Speaker, the law is not applied or established only after someone has committed a murder. The law exists, and nobody in unaware of that. The citizen is free to respect the law or to break it. But should he transgress it, should he commit a murder, he will know in advance that the law will punish him.
Mr. Speaker, the minister says capital punishment should be abolished "in the name of God", but if Marcotte the "Santa Claus" who fired point-blank and coldly at policemen, were released today from the Montreal penitentiary after having served a seven, eight or ten year sentence and if the Solicitor General needed an honest and loyal employee, would he hire Marcotte? Surely not. Not a single business man, not a single employer would trust a murderer.
But for the sake of society and of humanitarianism, the minister says capital punishment should be abolished "in the name of God" in order to help a family. Those are false arguments, that is stupid reasoning.
Mr. Speaker, the Creditistes will not make a political stock argument out of that. Let us not play politics with it. When it was decided in this House that there would be a free vote on the bill on capital punishment, we were pleased to hear the government give us that promise and that is why Mr. Brown, the lawyer, advises us to get together, Liberals, Progressive Conservatives, NDP members-if there are some against abolition-and Creditistes, to prevent this bill from being passed by the House.
Mr. Speaker, those are the remarks I wanted to make. I have letters, another one here from Chatham, Ontario-

We support your stand on capital punishment-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my colleague for at least letting me conclude my remarks. I shall be brief.
I received another letter favouring the retention of capital punishment. It is from Mr. Lawrence P. Ripley, 7730, 23rd Avenue, Montreal. Mr. Ripley also talks about the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). Would Mr. Ripley not be living in the minister's constituency? I quote:

Mr. Allmand described the cruel form of execution used in Spain. He did not describe the many cruel ways that a murderer uses such as a gun, a knife, strangulation, a club, rape or, worst of all, death by fire.

The minister ought to know that when a bandit armed with a submachine gun enters a bank, it is neither to say his rosary nor to do the stations of the cross, in God's name. When he does, his mind is set on killing if his robbery fails. The minister should think about this for a while. When he reasons this way, I cannot help wonder who his advisors are or whether the Holy Ghost is inspiring him in his sleep.
At any rate, we are investigating this matter everywhere in Canada. I was in western Canada during the last weekend, specifically in Edmonton and Vancouver, where I was asked lots of questions about capital punishment. I claim that 90 per cent of our population favour retention.
I have before me a letter from Mrs. Katherine Cordaro, from Georgetown, Ont., which is not even my riding. I quote:

There are many, many people who will back you all the way in your comments on capital punishment.

Mr. Speaker, I could quote letters all day long and pursue the debate until next week to demonstrate how much the people are in favour of maintaining capital punishment. Again, I shall repeat it: I hear New Democratic Party members speak about the humanitarian feelings we should show towards murderers and say that we should not kill those murderers but when we speak about abortion or the murder of a young child in his mother's womb, a child who never committed a murder, who never harmed anyone, who never asked to be born, they blame us. In the one hand, they say: kill the baby who did nothing wrong but protect the bandit who killed his fellowman.
As far as capital punishment is concerned, logic was certainly not born in New Democratic Party ranks.
Mr. Speaker, I have here another letter from Mr. Alvin S. Nemetz, Mississauga, near Toronto. The Solicitor General and the member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) received copies of that letter. I quote:
Sir:
I regret that more urgent matters have kept me from commenting earlier on the matter of capital punishment.
October 18, 1973

I cannot possibly express adequately my disgust and disappointment upon finding that our government has sunk so low as to be guilty of a flagrant breach of ethics. Mr. Allmand's action in radically altering the bill after it received second reading strips him of any right to ever discuss or comment on ethics, morality or justice. In permitting him to do so, you have once again revealed your utter contempt for parliament and the Canadian public.
[ Transla tion]
That letter was sent to the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau and copies were sent to three other members of parliament, including the Solicitor General.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, I could quote letters all day long. I would like to quote a leading article on capital punishment:
He who infringes social order deprives himself of the right to live or to be free, by committing his offence;
It is not the government, it is not members of parliament. It is he who infringes social order who deprives himself of the right to live or to be free. He is aware of it. Therefore, if he is aware of it, he must act consequently. I go on quoting:
-through the execution of the punishment, it is the property of life or freedom to which he was no longer entitled that is taken away from him in fact".
And many comments, articles, editorials, support the retention of capital punishment.
I would like now to quote a circular coming from Toronto:

This letter is from Miss Rita Hogg, president, Concerned Residents Action Committee:
We urge retentionist members to keep up the excellent work they are doing for we are more than ever convinced by the trend of events in our society today that it is indeed time to reinstate capital punishment.
Then a postscript:
Your leadership and solidarity have accomplished a very great deal. We are grateful to you. Keep up the good work.

This circular letter was sent to many parliament members. Probably the Solicitor General received it also. Perhaps he will speak during the debate on the amendments before us but many competent people spoke in the past; today they speak again in favour of the retention of capital punishment.
I am looking at the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) in his seat. When he was Minister of Justice for the province of Quebec, he was in favour of retaining capital punishment and after it was abolished, five years ago, he still was for retention. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe is as good a lawyer as the Solicitor General. He was Minister of Justice in Quebec; it is a position as important as that of Solicitor General but the latter is speaking in the name of God. In the name of God we want justice to be rendered; we want a murderer to be punished for his crime against society. It is not as a vengeance but for a better respect of law and for the respect of the human beings who want to live in peace and order in our Canadian society.
Criminal Code

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion that I have spoken on this measure and I trust that it will be the last. I am now speaking to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), and as I intend to speak only the once I trust I shall be able to exercise some leeway in regard to the aspects of the bill with which I wish to deal and also the amendments.
First of all, this bill is a very confusing piece of legislation. There is no need for it to be confusing. One would think the simple question whether or not certain persons should be put to death if they commit certain offences is straightforward. Yet we find ourselves in a peculiar position when we take a look at Bill C-2.
The legislation states that a certain section of the Criminal Code in the Revised Statutes of Canada will be repealed and the following substituted therefor:
214. (1) Murder is punishable by death or is punishable by imprisonment for life.
If you gave the bill to a person not used to the intricacies and the tortuous method of passing legislation through this House, I am sure that person would assume that this bill calls for capital punishment. "Murder is punishable by death", says the bill. Only through the machinations and confused operations of the present government could they have managed to bring forward a bill that calls for punishment by death and yet places parliament in a position where the retentionists are going to vote against the bill and the abolitionists are going to vote for the bill, which as I say calls for "murder punishable by death".
Given the premise that we start with a bill that says exactly the opposite to what it is supposed to say, a lot of extra difficulties have been created as a result, and totally unnecessarily. The original amendments which were submitted received a fair amount of forethought, I believe. I am sorry that the amendment asking for a plebiscite was ruled out of order because I would have voted in favour of it had it been possible to do so.
The hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) has asked for an extension of the classes of murder which could be punishable by death. I am inclined to agree that if one accepts the philosophy that murder should ever be punishable by death, then one death is not greatly different from another provided there is the intention to murder someone. While I respect the right of a policeman on duty and penitentiary guards to ask for extra protection, I feel it is possibly a more heinous crime to murder defenceless children than it is to have a shoot-out with a policeman. But this is a matter of personal opinion and I would find no difficulty in supporting the amendment moved by the hon. lady from Louis-Hebert. Having accepted the principle that it is possible to put a person to death for certain types of murder, I do not see the logic of trying to be quite as narrow as this bill is in regard to what types of murder should be punishable by death.
For the most part, the debate so far has been conducted with a fair amount of reason. Members appear to be divided into roughly three divisions. Retentionists are

quite happy to retain capital punishment. On their outer fringe, they appear to want to have people put to death. On the other extreme are the abolitionists who appear to have been born that way. They have never been required to search their conscience on that matter. The third group is centered between those two. They do not wish people to be put to death, but they see no reasonable or possible alternative. Others will not vote for retention.
I am disappointed in the amount of intolerance both in the corridors and in the speeches by members of all parties. One would expect the abolitionists to be a little more tolerant of the views of their colleagues than has been evidenced. I say this with a great deal of regret.
I sometimes believe that I must be the only individual in Canada who did not spend his time talking about capital punishment before becoming involved in politics. I can honestly say that I never expressed an opinion on whether we should have capital punishment until the election campaign got under way. The first few times I was asked for my view about capital punishment I was inclined to say it was my own business. That is not so. I was a candidate for political office and people presumed they had a right to inquire into my views on the subject. On consideration, I believe they were correct. They have a right to know how a candidate is going to vote on a matter such as this, although I am surprised people would change their votes for candidates for the House of Commons depending on how they were going to vote on capital punishment. I would think a voter would be interested in how a candidate was going to vote on capital punishment but, with all the other important issues with which we are involved, I was surprised to hear many people say that if I voted for abolition they would not vote for me or if I voted for retention they would not vote for me. There seemed to have been an equal division. My letters indicated they would or would not vote for people because of their vote on this measure. I am also sorry to report that.
A member of parliament must decide whether he is better qualified than his constituents in this matter, if we are going to go by the results of polls and letters. If a member of parliament is convinced he has a more highly qualified opinion on this matter than the average constituent, he should have no hesitation in voting whichever way he feels. I, personally, do not feel that way. I have no qualification that would enable me to say that I have better judgment on whether a person should be put to death for certain crimes than anyone in my constituency. The person with a menial job and perhaps very little in the way of education might very well be right on this issue and I might be wrong. Consequently, I do not hesitate to accept the wishes of my constituents in this matter as I can determine them. I make no apology for so doing.
I feel that democracy is exercised all too seldom in this country and surely the basis of democracy is rule by the people. In a matter such as this, I have no hesitation in accepting the advice of the overwhelming majority of my constituents. There are other issues on which I do not hesitate to go against the wishes of the majority of my constituents. I have done so on two occasions in this parliament. It is a matter of what you consider to be your qualifications.

I have travelled a great deal in Canada and have rubbed shoulders with many different groups of people in various parts of the country. In certain matters of national import I believe I am better qualified than the average constituent in Victoria. I hope I will not be thought too conceited for that remark. One of the measures I am referring to is, of course, the official languages bill.
During this debate we have heard a great deal about Edmund Burke. For many years I have been fond of reading his speeches. I have always considered that he put words together in a manner that should be an example to everyone using the English language. I recommend his speeches to all. However, I think they have been used during this debate in a manner he would not have defended.
Mr. Burke was born an Irish Catholic. In 1774, he was elected to parliament at Westminster to represent the constituency of Bristol. He represented it very well for six years. In 1780, he found to his horror that the people of Bristol were not likely to renominate him. He then made his famous speech in the Guild Hall in Bristol, a speech that is often quoted and frequently misquoted in this House. It is often said that because Burke was willing to vote against the wishes of his constituents we should do the same. However, Burke did this on the very type of matter I have been talking about, a matter on which he was an expert. He went against his constituents on matters where their prejudices were prevalent, the Irish question and the American revolution.
I always thought his best speeches were on the American revolution where he took a very tolerant attitude early in the revolution and suggested there should be some compromise. He also voted according to his wisdom on the Catholic relief bill and the Irish trade bill. I think he was quite right in doing so. He had more wisdom and knowledge on these matters than his constituents, so he voted the way he felt. He pointed this out to them.
Early in his so often quoted speech in the Guild Hall he said that by all means he should consider the wishes of his constituents wherever possible and on those matters on which his constituents were knowledgeable he should consult their opinions. However, in matters where he had superior knowledge and intellect and had studied and worked, he felt quite at liberty, as do I, to vote according to his own knowledge and intelligence. As a footnote, I should add that after Mr. Burke's great speech that is so often quoted he lost the nomination and was never again truly elected. He did not get the nomination and from then on represented a private constituency owned by the Duke of Rockingham. So while he went down in history in respect of this one speech, he was a failure in a political sense.
Another thing that happened in the early stages of the debate on capital punishment was that capital punishment was linked to the question of law and order. At first I rejected this and said that the two were different subjects. I said that capital punishment is a subject by itself when we consider whether or not we will take the life of a human being because the state wishes us so to do. The matter kept coming up and I began to wonder if perhaps I
October 18, 1973

might be wrong and that the two are rightly linked. I was impressed by a column written by Richard Needham who regularly writes for the Globe and Mail. I refer to an article that was syndicated in a Victoria newspaper on September 17, I believe. He was speaking of the lack of religion in our society. I think the article was headed "Nothing Is Sacred". He mentioned that in this day and age more and more crimes, such as murder, robbery, rape and so on, occurred in churches. There was the case of a Canadian minister who was set upon in New York City while walking from one church across the street to another. Mr. Needham quoted Dostoyevsky. His version was quite abridged. I believe the entire quotation is worthwhile. It was written some time in the mid-19th century. Dostoyesky wrote as follows:
If you were to destroy in mankind the belief in immortality, not only love but every living force maintaining the life of the world would at once be dried up. Moreover, nothing then would be immoral, everything would be permissible, even cannibalism.
In his abridgement I believe Mr. Needham said, "if there is no God, anything is permissible". I believe we have a situation today in this country that the strictures and standards that had been set for so many years, based on the law of Moses, the Ten Commandments, and which served as a structure for our social and moral life, are considered today by younger people and some not so young as being irrelevant. However, there is nothing to replace those strictures that were impressed upon people with the effect that they believed if they were evil they would suffer damnation thereafter. Several other people have been quoted on this subject. I suppose one of the best examples is Voltaire who said that if God did not exist we would have to invent him. When so many of our people appear to no longer believe in or accept religion, the lawmakers must bring in some kind of philosophy for the people to replace these strictures. We have failed miserably in this regard.
I spoke to a friend of mine in the New Democratic Party yesterday, who unfortunately is not in the House today, who said he has no problem in this regard because he believes in the rule of law and that he has almost made this belief the equivalent of that held by people who believe in the law of God. In other words, if you worship the law then you need no other strictures on your behaviour. I find that this goes a bit far, but we are faced with this dilemma and I do not know how to solve it to everyone's satisfaction. I am sure there are greater thinkers than I who are worrying about this problem. When we look round the House we realize that there are 264 members who are placed in the position of trying to represent the collective wisdom of the country. I think there may be better judges of the problem facing us or of the rightness or wrongness in respect of this matter. But it is now our responsibility.
Many members of the House have participated in state killings. I am speaking of world war II when we were sent out and, after a certain amount of what modern-day persons refer to as "being psyched up" to something, found ourselves able to take lives on behalf of the state with no particular qualms of conscience. I suppose years later some of us worried about it. However, it was done at the time. Incidentally, I was chosen to participate in the execution of General Kurt Meyer which was to be carried out
Criminal Code
by the Canadian forces in 1946. I approached this as another job. It did not bother me a great deal. I am sure, had we gone through with the execution, it would not have bothered me a great deal. As I say, we were psyched up, and we were young.
This debate has bothered me a great deal. I am sure it has bothered most members. I am glad it is coming to an end. I intend to vote against the bill on third reading. I shall vote against the amendment which is before us now largely because I do not care for its wording. The part I am most unhappy about is the part in which a second murder is not spelled out as murder but as the death of a human being. It seems to me this amendment would have to be further amended to indicate that the second taking of life must be murder. I suggest to the hon. member for North-umberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) that since the second part of the amendment states, "in respect of any person, where such person causes the death of a human being and has been previously convicted of murder, whether or not such murder is punishable by death", it seems to me that this would not cover the situation where a person convicted of murder, not punishable by death, was involved in an automobile accident which resulted in the death of a person. Such a situation, I suggest, should be excluded from this provision. Had the word "murder" been included I would have supported the amendment. However, I do not think it has much chance of being passed. I shall vote against the bill at the third reading stage. I hope we can then forget the quarrels and bitterness and go on from there.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I propose to speak very briefly. I shall confine my remarks entirely to the amendment. The amendment presented by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) represents a conscious attempt to try to pull some reason out of a bill with which even the minister was not satisfied. When he appeared before the committee he tried to amend the bill all over again by changing its very nature and status. The committee was really stirred up. An effort was made to put forward an amendment in connection with euthanasia. The hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham tried to put forward that amendment. He said: "Let us get rid of the rope. Let us not be cruel in exercising the death penalty." That is not before us, unfortunately, because again it was blocked by procedure. At that time there was no reason whatsoever why the minister should not have admitted that there is disagreement and confusion in the country and that this legislation will affect every citizen in Canada. But what did the minister do? He said that in no way is he forcing it through but that it has to go through in the way he says it should and that what the people of Canada are saying does not matter.
I commend the hon. member for Northumberland-Dur-ham and the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) for their amendments because both these hon. members have been trying to present to the House some form of compromise. It is well known that right across Canada people demand the reinstatement of the maximum penalty because they are disturbed and incensed at the fact that some people can go out and murder and get nothing more than a nice sentence to a comfortable jail. We know that something must be inserted into our criminal law that will satisfy the people of Canada. Those hon. members have tried to do that in their amendments.
I hope that the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) will change his mind and vote for these amendments tonight. I hope that hon. members opposite and members of the NDP who have been adamant against capital punishment will say that at least we have reflected to some extent the opinion of our constituents. We have said that those who murder in the course of airline hijackings, which is a heinous crime, should be subject to the death penalty as well as those who have murdered again following escape from those nice, tight secure jails of the present Solicitor General. Surely these people have lost their right to be in our society.
These amendments are not good amendments; they are makeshift amendments because the bill is a makeshift bill. It should have been withdrawn and rewritten from scratch. The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham and the hon. member for Louis-Hebert have put forward these amendments to try to make some sense out of the bill and to try to solve the problems because it does not do so. But what does the minister do? He does not want these amendments. He does not want the Criminal Code of Canada to reflect the morality of Canadians and the desire of Canadians for the kind of punishment which they feel should be in their statutes.
I do not intend to say much at this time about the concept and the reason for capital punishment being in the Criminal Code. I may speak about that later in the debate on third reading of the bill. But at this point let me plead with hon. members to realize that these amendments, particularly the amendment of the hon. member for North-

umberland-Durham, do make sense and will at least allow some hon. members who really do not want to see capital punishment contained in the Criminal Code to say to their constituents and to the people of Canada that they as members of the House were at least responsible regarding the matter of double murder and murder during airline hijacking. The minister cannot refuse to listen to the people. This House is not an ivory tower, although members to the left of me continue to think it is. Surely we can accept this small compromise, this small bone, if you want to put it that way, tossed out by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham. At least we will have shown that we pay attention to the people of Canada. If we do not do so as members who represent the people of Canada I suggest that some of us had better find another job, perhaps join the ministry or become social workers. They had better not continue being members of parliament because obviously they do not really want to listen to the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the members
Veterans Affairs

I am referring to the unveiling and dedication of the Newfoundland Book of Remembrance which, after the dedication, will be placed, along with the four other Books of Remembrance, in the Memorial Chamber of the Peace Tower.

Joseph Harnum, Lieutenant-Governor of Newfoundland and Mr. Frank Moores, Premier of Newfoundland. Mr. Speaker, once more I rise to take part in the debate on Bill C-2 and to support the amendment in the name of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) and the one in the name of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence). I doubt whether at this point our speeches are likely to change the minds of many hon. members of this House.
We can address ourselves to our constituents, or to those in the gallery; we can speak to the fourth estate or to the public at large, but it boils down to one factor-the 264 members of this House who will be making up their minds and deciding what is to happen to the measure before us. Many of us could be quoted as saying, "My mind is made up. Don't confuse me with the facts." I believe I have mentioned this before. Everything that can be said has been said many times. speechtext:
As one favouring retention, I am against hanging. I believe it is a terrible and barbaric way of execution. But in the final analysis, when crimes have been committed such as those outlined in the motion of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert, such as rape killings, capital punishment must be applied and it must be administered as painlessly as possible. I think this is the feeling that should be presented to members of the House. I am aware that this is an emotional subject. I am also aware, as are all hon. members, that the overwhelming majority of the people of Canada are in favour of, and in fact are demanding, the retention of capital punishment.
There are some very fine members, even some not in our party, who are abolitionists and I should like to see some of them come back after the next election. This is why I hope they will give second thought to the amendments to this bill when they are finally voted upon. Whether they realize it or not, our constituents are very concerned about this question. It is all very well for the most knowledgeable members to speak at great length and to say they know a good deal better than their constituents what is good for the people they represent. That is possibly so in

certain complicated cases. But there is nothing complicated about this capital punishment bill, or as our friends in the for th estate and on television call it, this hanging bill. This is not a hanging bill; it is a not hanging bill.
The press and other members of the media would by a great majority favour abolition if a poll were taken of them. As a result, their news forecasts have been slanted, and let no one think that is not so. I have not yet seen today's newspapers, but I am sure that in some papers across Canada we will be seeing grisly cartoons portraying the terrible aspects of capital punishment. We have all seen cartoons of the cold, grey dawn, the noose and the scaffold. A great many of us who are in favour of capital punishment are at the same time opposed to hanging. We just want to see murderers dispatched as painlessly and as quickly as possible once they are found guilty of murder in the first degree.
One newscaster earlier this year, when reading the news made no mention of Bill C-2; again there was reference to the "hanging bill," and portrayed behind him was the noose and the scaffold. In all fairness, he might just as well have portrayed a murdered child or elderly person on the screen behind him. Let us not kid ourselves; the media can shape public opinion and they have done so. As I have said before, and as many hon. members have agreed, the media have never been able to sell the Canadian people on abolition of the death penalty in Canada: about 90 per cent of the people are still in favour of capital punishment.
Some members of the House to whom I have spoken since returning here indicated that they have received a great deal of flak, shall I say, or criticism from their constituents. One of our members this morning said he had had a change of heart, that he would be supporting the amendment and voting against the bill. If my memory serves me correctly, 138 members voted in favour of this bill on May 29, and 114 voted against. That is a difference of 24. So those of us who feel that law and order is necessary, and that we must retain capital punishment in the law of Canada, have only to talk to 13 people and get them to change their vote in order to defeat this bill, which is the wish of the people of Canada as the government is well aware. I am sure the Solicitor General knows the feelings of the ordinary citizens of Canada. The percentage in favour of retention runs anywhere from 90 per cent to the most conservative estimate, with a small "c" of 60 to 70 per cent.
Millions of words have been printed on this subject. Whether or not the people in the cities are aware of it, people in rural Canada are very concerned about their safety, about the fact that law and order is not what it should be in this age of permissiveness. As a result, I am sure if this parliament in its wisdom decided to defeat Bill C-2, this would truly reflect the wishes, indeed the demands, of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the two amendments now before the House are an indication that some modification must take place in relation to those in society to whom the death penalty should apply. I listened to the speech made by the mover of the second amendment and was surprised to hear him say that if he were able to get it accepted, he would vote against the main bill that he was amending. What he is suggesting is

that if a person commits murder, following which he serves a term of imprisonment, having been tried and convicted, and is released and commits a second murder, he should be hanged. Since he has already said that he wants them to be hanged the first time, that seems to me to be an anomaly.
His second point concerned the hanging of people who hijack aircraft. If there was ever a field in which more hysteria has been developed, with less justification, it is in the field of hijacking. In a very short period of time many countries passed a convention which was acceptable to most.
