The hon. member says it is unenforceable. That is true. It is a bit like riots. You can make a lot of pious statements about prohibiting riots or you can read the riot act. You can do that with hijacking. The point I want to make is that hijacking is carried out for many reasons. The first is monetary. Some hijackers have held up aircraft for very large ransoms. That is the worst possible type of abuse. In my opinion countries should not bargain on that basis. The company that owns the aircraft should not be permitted to pay the ransom. The safety of everyone on board is sacrificed because the aircraft is worth $5 million, $7 million or $10 million. No price is put on the lives of the people on board. A great deal of hysteria has been built up around hijacking; therefore it is very easy to include this matter as an amendment to the bill before us. It involves something that is fundamental to this debate: either you are in favour of the death penalty or you are not.
When the five-year moratorium on the death penalty for murder in Canada was originally introduced, protection was given to prison guards and policemen. That was a bit like saying, "We are going to have a war, but we must provide special protection for the soldiers." However, it is the civilian, the innocent bystander who is not trained to protect himself. Civilians are not involved and in many cases are not even familiar with the problem. I was never in favour of providing that kind of protection even to satisfy those trying to put a stumbling-block in the way of total abolition. I always felt the prison guards knew what they were doing. Also, a policeman knows what he is doing. He would not command the salary he is receiving today if it were not for the fact he is taking a risk. Anyone who is afraid of being shot at should not be a policeman. Most policemen are not shot at, but they know there is that possibility. Soldiers do not think they will be killed; very few would go to war if they thought they would be. We originally had these exceptions, and now we are dealing with more exceptions in this bill.
What really bothers me is the attitude of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). If he had minded his own business and did what he started out to do, namely, asked that the moratorium be extended for another five years, that would have been fine. I am sure there would not have been this great hue and cry. There certainly would not have been the two amendments that are before us today. There are other amendments that have not yet have been reached which are just as foolish. One is the female
Capital Punishment
chauvinist amendment. Each amendment adds another exception and I object to them.
I was prompted to rise today by the statement of the Solicitor General. He calmly told this House that because of the great problem of overcrowding he is prepared to build more penitentiaries. However, he does not have the guts to fire Mr. Street, the man responsible for the overcrowding. The parole board is inoperative. Instead of doing something about the parole board, the minister is asking parliament to add more people to it. You can have all the people you want on the parole board, but unless a certain percentage of prisoners are released on parole in an orderly fashion it does not matter a hoot.
The minister said an additional penitentiary will be built in British Columbia and that he is looking for land for another one. He must have a hole in his head. The minister should be the last to bring forward this type of legislation. An easy way for him to get rid of some of the people in penitentiaries would be to hang them. Why has he brought forward this piece of legislation? By regulation, the minister has made it mandatory that a person convicted of murder be committed to the penitentiary for ten years. It is also suggested that the judge will be allowed to add to that an additional ten years. The minister talks about building more penitentiaries. If he continues with this kind of legislation we will have the biggest building boom in history; we will not be able to keep up with building new penitentiaries because of the numbers waiting to get into them.
By providing a mandatory prison sentence we do not allow the parole system to operate. If we are really that backward, we should do what the retentionists say-let's go back to an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. If a person does something wrong, put him in jail. I presume the Solicitor General is in favour of bringing back the paddle, the lash and all the other things that go with an obsolete penal reform system.
The question is, not how many exceptions there should be but whether anyone should be hanged. It hinges on whether society believes in an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. If so, it means there is no penal reform. It means the Solicitor General will be right in saying that more penitentiaries will have to be built. In that case we may accomplish something in this country which no other civilized society has ever done; we may have the largest percentage of persons in penitentiaries of any country in the world. That is a possibility. If Mr. Street remains in control of the parole board, we will certainly be heading in the direction of accomplishing that. Also, this Solicitor General has done more than his share in that regard.
Surely, in a country as advanced as Canada we do not believe in the argument of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Surely, we believe that people can be rehabilitated. One of my colleagues told me today that he visited the penitentiary in Prince Albert. He told a very interesting story about a man who had been in solitary confinement, and segregated from the other inmates for a number of years. He said when the man got out, he was crazy. Obviously, the court did not decide he was crazy or he would not have been sentenced for the crime. However, from a layman's point of view something is wrong with this person, yet he is released and may do whatever he did

October 18, 1973
Capital Punishment
before because we have not really helped him. We do not help him by punishing him. We help him by attempting to fit him back into society. I am sure no one would suggest that we have penitentiaries for any other reason than to contain people who stray from the norms of society. They are contained there not for their own sake but for the benefit of society.
We place a person in segregation, we leave him there for a period of years, then at the end of his sentence we allow him to come out of segregation-where he was kept because he was considered too dangerous to mingle with the other inmates-and we put him on the street. When we do this, something must be wrong with our heads. If there is a mad dog in a pound it is ridiculous for the poundkeep-er to say, "We cannot train him, therefore we will put him on the street." I do not think anyone in this House would agree that a man who for years has been segregated in a penitentiary because he is dangerous is suddenly eligible to be put on the street. However, that is what we do. In many cases we put on the street a man who is considered by all the guards and most of the prisoners in the institution to be mentally unbalanced.
The minister has done very little in this regard. He has not done anything about classification officers or improvement of psychiatric treatment. He has not done anything in co-operation with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), who plays with wheat instead of looking after the Department of Justice. The Minister of Justice should be making a decision in respect of changes in sentencing people. He should be taking steps so they may be refitted into society. This is what the parole board is supposed to do but it is not what it has been doing. The members of the parole board have been going around talking to these people. It is like a premiere performance in a theatre. The man has been waiting for the day when the parole board will interview him at the penitentiary. He has rehearsed and thought about what he will say. He has been doing this for weeks and weeks. He has a command performance before the board. If there is anything more phony than this situation, I fail to see it. The inmate puts on his grand performance and the members of the parole board say, "Sonny, you can go home because we think you are reformed" or, "We do not like the show you put on, so you had better go back and try again later".
Surely we should look at the problem. There are members of the Conservative Party who say they stand for law and order. They stand for law and order like Spiro Agnew. The case of Spiro Agnew is a very good example of law and order. This is a man who should have kept his mouth shut because he had his hand in the till. I am not suggesting that the Conservatives are in that position, but they may be looking at the past rather than today in respect of this problem. It is a fact that very few people murder a second time. It is also a fact, with the exception of political terrorists, that very few people have been killed in hijackings. Hon. members know that with relation to the number of people carried by international airlines, the number of people killed is infinitesimal.
They must know that very few people have been murdered in Canada during the last 20 or 30 years. They must also know that most of us believe in law and order. Most

Canadians are proud of the fact that one can walk down the street in most of our communities at night without any danger of being robbed, mugged or raped. This is not true in other countries. It does not have anything to do with the death penalty, the penitentiary system or anything else. It is an attitude of society. It is interesting that in places like England where there are large populations in concentrated areas, the members of the police forces are not armed and very seldom are the gangsters armed. We also find that robbery with violence is seldom carried out.
I suggest that the people of Canada who stand for law and order should not relate this to belief in an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. There is a more enlightened way. If the authors of the Bible were to return today, I am sure they would write it in a different way. I am sure they would not be in favour of stoning people and many of the other things which took place. We are asking for public hanging again, in the name of law and order. There is no record to indicate that this has an effect on law and order.
I suggest these amendments only add to the two or three exceptions we now have. The issue, really, is not whether more murderers should be given the death penalty; it is, rather, that we should face the problem in respect of law and order. We should face these problems as they develop. This the Solicitor General has not done. We should start to rehabilitate people on the day we put them in jail. We should provide them with sex in the penitentiaries and all the other amenities of society before we release them.
If there is anything that bothers the average Canadian, it is the differing treatment given to people in penitentiaries. What happened in respect of Mr. Ballard? He was a white-collar prisoner so he received the best treatment. What does the blue-collar prisoner get? He does not get the same treatment. He does not receive the type of legal counsel provided for Mr. Ballard, because the legal advice provided to him is free or almost free. Now we have the situation where Mr. Ballard gets out. He does not give the money back. Perhaps the income tax people will collect some of it on a sliding scale. We give him all the advantages. He is not asked to go into the ordinary penitentiary; the penitentiary people placed him in a halfway house, with a quarterway house just down the street. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am still puzzled about the amendments to Bill C-2, because they apparently show that we are far from agreeing on the basic principle of the legislation seeking to abolish the death penalty. It is wished to abolish capital punishment while admitting criminal liability in a larger number of cases so as to punish with capital punishment the truly capital murders. Therefore, this dilemma always brings us back to the basic questions which we must ask ourselves in order to decide how we should consider this bill.
Of course, I shall repeat what I said at an earlier stage of the debate on this bill: does our present society deserve to have capital punishment abolished? Is our society prepared to admit that we should abolish capital punishment? It is most important since it could be demonstrated ad absurdum that if an individual does not commit any murder, there is no need to discuss capital punishment. This, of course, is what we would like.
Even if capital punishment were maintained, even if we could improve society to the point where capital murder would no longer exist, it would not be applied.
Therefore, since the great majority of Canadians are in favour of retaining capital punishment-this seems obvious and a referendum would actually prove it no doubt- and even though we should ask ourselves whether our society is prepared to agree to abolition, we should choose retention instead while shaping the law so that crime would disappear from our society.
Mr. Speaker, this has not yet materialized. We have not yet passed enough measures in favour of the true freedom and development of the individual so that crime may disappear, but unfortunately we have not yet reached that point. But we must judge in a concrete way and say: Well, since in society, even modern society, wanton crime still exists, therefore society does not deserve the abolition of the death penalty. And it is society itself which can alone determine whether it must be abolished or not since all society has to do is to ensure that there are no more murderers, and even if one law maintained capital punishment, that law would obviously never be enforced.
Capital Punishment
In my view, it would be a mistake to abolish capital punishment on all kinds of more or less humanitarian pretexts. We would be ill-advised; we should follow rather the very evolution of society.
On the other hand, the study of the amendments now before us shows that we want the abolition of capital punishment, but that it should be maintained in such and such a case. Judgments would then have to be much more accurate and complete, which means that all the cases in which there really is a capital crime, where the crime is really foul and truly deserves the supreme punishment, should be accurately described. They would all have to be listed. Since there is the danger of forgetting some, it is much easier not to list all the cases and instead of reestablishing capital punishment, to amend the legislation so that each murder case be judged on its own value and that the judge may consider all the facts and decide whether there really was a crime, whether it was a capital or a foul murder or whether it was simply a case of self-defense, of accident, or manslaughter, etc. In fact, only judges can pass judgements in such cases once they are aware of all the facts. If they rule that the accused does not deserve capital punishment, they will simply pass judgement in consequence. And when they decide that a murder warrants capital punishment, they will give the sentence accordingly.
I think that presently that is the only logical way to consider capital punishment, that is to judge each case on its own true merit, under the real circumstances, so we will not continuously be forced to amend the law. That would make it truly possible to punish those who commit the most heinous crime there is.
The examination of those amendments leads us to that type of reflection, and that is why I say that we are getting lost in all that. In fact, why inflict capital punishment on a double murderer, as the amendment says, that would mean doing away with only one person who has already done away with two. It could be in both cases that they were not real capital murderers but because two crimes have been committed the supreme punishment would be approved. I find that still ambiguous. That is why we try by all possible means to bring the government to specify a few cases that could satisfy public opinion, the great majority of which favours the retention of capital punishment.
I think that we are simply losing our time and that it would be much simpler to do what most people want, that is maintain capital punishment and have each case judged in all justice to avoid forever misunderstandings or errors-we must come to that-that could lead to somebody being sentenced unjustly. I fully agree with that but, on the other hand, I think in today's society we must really punish those who deserve to be, and I would even say want to be, since when we deal with real murderers who are very dangerous, one can say that the role of society is nothing else than to get rid of them. We must not either establish a distinction that might be unfair, because when we say, as this legislation does, that capital punishment is maintained in cases of murders of prison guards or policemen, we are being unfair, in my opinion, to all other groups of people who have the same value and

October 18, 1973
Capital Punishment
who, besides, Mr. Speaker, may happen to find themselves in situations similar to those of policemen and prison guards. I refer in particular to bank managers, cashiers, all these people who never know when they can expect to face gangsters. In my view, these people run the same risk and even more-since they usually do not carry any gun- as policemen or prison guards who expect such a situation and who therefore carry a gun and may defend themselves more easily, as part of their job.
Therefore, this provision in the case of murders of policemen and prison guards is, in my view, unfair to all other groups of citizens and I do not believe that our role in this chamber is to establish such distinctions. And if we look at statistics, Mr. Speaker, we realize that there are no more murders of policemen and prison guards than of any other group of citizens. For instance I referred to one particular group: bank employees. Even a businessman may at a given time be subject to the cupidity of gangsters and his life can be even more jeopardized than that of policemen.
I wonder then why he should not have the same advantages or he would not be under the act in the same way as policemen and prison guards. Thus the law contains something abnormal if not unfair and the only correction we should bring now would simply be to reinstate or maintain capital punishment but we could spell out for the judge the way prosecutions would have to be conducted in order to discover among all the murderers in general those whose crimes deserve the supreme punishment. I think this is the part we should play, and so we would agree with those who accept it. As our society breeds murderers, we have to respect the view of the vast majority of citizens and maintain capital punishment. Consequently, I do not think the amendments refine the act in any way and if they did, we should introduce many other amendments in order to determine all cases of murder deserving death punishment. But then we risk forgetting certain categories of crimes and, once again, to be unfair. This is why by simply maintaining capital punishment and judging each case on its own according to the circumstances, we could be fairer towards everyone and we could faithfully reflect the general views of all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have liked this morning to take part in the debate and I would have thought that we could perhaps have discussed the two amendments which were before us, since there is a rather close connection between both. However, we must accept the Speaker's decision, but it was ignored as soon as it was given, since almost anything has been discussed. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) launched a scathing attack against the Parole Board. We have heard many other things. Several of my colleagues in the House have spoken to the bill as a whole rather than to the amendments. I would have liked to speak during the debate, because I could have easily-and I am going to do so-supported the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) as well as that of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) although I find some difficulties in its wording, especially concerning the proposed paragraph c) on the second death.


I did not speak on second reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker. Some people may complain that this debate has been going on for a very long time, but I point out that it has taken place bit by bit. It started in January with the minister's speech proposing this amending bill. Then there were possibly two days of debate in February and, lo and behold, some debate in April, some in May, some in June and some in July. The government introduced the bill in January and I cannot for the life of me understand why it did not continue to deal with it at that time.
Probably these comments should be made on third reading. However, I believe that in dealing with this bill the minister has been flying kites, testing the wind and then retreating in face of the violent reaction of public opinion. Canadians, in the great majority of cases, disagree wholeheartedly with this bill and with the manner in which the administration of justice has been carried out by the government. It is like a man trying to test the temperature of his bath. He puts in his big toe, but the water is too hot so he removes his foot. He dances around a few times, as this government has done, and then puts his toe in again. This House went by dribs and drabs, and then we had that ludicrous performance in the committee hearings. I say that in all seriousness.
I know the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) is very serious and is dedicated to his job, but I suggest to him and to the administration, if it was in support of his move, that the amendment the minister put in committee was in violent contempt of parliament. I am not casting any reflection on the minister as to his own personal qualities, but he did not have the political guts, or the administration did not, to put that amendment or proposition to the House instead of asking the House to vote on a bill which was to be a mere extension. In addition, he then offered suckers or lollipops to soothe the objections of some of the abolitionists and also perhaps throwing a sop to those who believe the system was releasing convicted murderers and putting them back into society.
There were some unfortunate incidents as a result of that policy of sort of trial and error. Some uninformed, unintelligent ad hockery has been the history of this bill and what preceded it. Then there was the attempt in committee to totally abolish the death sentence. Why did they think the committee was going to be pressured, that it could be packed, that there was not to be any free vote, that party pressures would be on? Since one party in the committee, as a party position, had decided to abolish capital punishment, were government representatives going to be pressured into voting for the Solicitor General's amendment? This is where I find that this line of conduct was totally unacceptable and less than respectable.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) made sense with some of his remarks this afternoon, but unfortunately his ideological blindspots took over and he went on a trip. He is right when he says that somewhere, somehow, in the minds of a lot of people this is a debate about the abolition of capital punishment. Of course, it is
October 18, 1973

not, because since 1967 the amendments to the Criminal Code have retained capital punishment.
People are wrong when they say that decision with regard to the abolition or retention of capital punishment is an exercise of the royal prerogative. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, with all due deference, that this is not flaunting the law, it is flouting the law-that this is no reflection upon the royal prerogative as such. Yet we know who exercises it. For a short time I was a part of the system and I think it is wrong. But I will talk about that on third reading. This has been said before; the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said it in his remarks on second reading even though he is a convinced abolitionist.
We could remove all restrictions on capital punishment, those that exist in the law that goes back to 1961, or only those that were in the amendments of 1967: we could go back prior to 1961 and it would not make any difference with an administration that says there shall be no hanging. They will rationalize and find every excuse, legitimate or otherwise, to justify a commutation. All the documentation is privileged and no one can really judge objectively whether the commutation was legitimate or not.
I am not attacking the personality of any past solicitor general. The cabinet members were entitled to their views and I do say that they held them honestly. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not think the system is right and therefore I come back to my charge. When the newspaper editorialists, columnists and the media in general refer to this as a debate on the abolition of capital punishment, they are wrong. This is merely a bill for restriction of the categories of crime for which capital punishment shall be the penalty or may be the penalty. That is all, so let us be honest.
If there is abolition de facto, it lies in the exercise of the royal prerogative. I know what the law was before 1961, and certainly the occasional death was carried out, but the pattern was evident before that: it depended upon the views of those who sat in cabinet-not upon the views of parliament but upon the views of the men who were the dominant personalities. I do not like a system of justice which has that basis, Mr. Speaker, but be that as it may.
The amendment put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), tries to respond, as does the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin), to public demand for a widening of the categories of murder to which the death penalty shall apply. This is a reduction of the so-called privilege of position, the privilege of right to life that is given to categories of persons in rather more hazardous walks of life, policemen on duty and prison guards. I will withhold my argument on that philosophical stance until later.
I fully agree that the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert is merely trying to reassert a portion of the law that exists today, that of capital punishment, for the unlawful taking of life during the commission of a crime of violence. The amendment refers to rape or attempted rape, but surely there could be added other crimes of violence. My colleague from Northumberland-Durham suggested hijacking, and I agree in a way with the hon. member for Timiskaming who said that this is in response
Capital Punishment
to public outcry. True enough, the crime is new and if it is a heinous crime let us recognize it as such; and if capital punishment is the answer to it in part, then so be it.
There is nothing so cowardly as a hijacker, whatever his motives may be. It may be a case, as the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) suggested, where some economic justification is supposed-a poor guy trying to get into the money. But I have never heard of that as a valid argument in favour of theft. Or it may be someone who feels that a political consideration justifies harming, threatening and even killing innocent persons who have no recourse. To this extent, I agree.
As to the second portion of the second amendment, I find the language a little difficult, though this might be corrected. The proposed amendment reads: in respect of any such person, where such person causes the death of a human being and has previously been convicted of murder-
Very well. Suppose a man has been convicted of noncapital murder and has served his sentence. He might be out on parole, or even that period of supervision might be over. And then he is convicted of manslaughter. Well, manslaughter certainly fits into the category of cases where a peson causes the death of a human being; the amendment does not say whether voluntarily or involuntarily, and to this extent the language is infelicitous. Be this as it may, it seems to me my hon. friend is responding to a public outcry which does not want society to be unprotected in such circumstances.
I can assure hon. members that the question of capital punishment loomed large as an issue on public platforms during the last election, at least in my part of the City of Edmonton. Unequivocal answers were demanded from candidates. The feeling was overwhelmingly in favour of the retention of the present law, that is, the 1961 amendments categorizing capital and non-capital murder. If the present administration were not so blind it would know this but, of course, the election results showed it was blind to public feeling, though the climate of opinion in western Canada was obvious. Thus, to the extent that these two amendments open up the bill-an ill-devised bill, in any case-1 intend to support them.

Mr. Speaker, I think we can all agree with the hon. member who preceded me that, on paper, the bill before us is not one which abolishes capital punishment. But I recall very well the remarks of the Solicitor-General (Mr. Allmand) when he introduced it on second reading. I think he used the words "de facto abolition". At least, we inferred from his remarks that the bill was one along the road to total abolition. I think it is more correct to put it in that way. He said the bill before us took us along the road to abolition.
I agree with this. I believe we should be moving along the road to abolition. Most of the debate which has taken place has been concerned with the narrow issue of the death penalty or its abolition. That is as it should be. I think that is what the public are interested in and what they wish us to discuss. Before us today are two amendments. The first would impose capital punishment on

October 18, 1973
Capital Punishment
those who commit a second murder. I think I am correct in saying that in the history of this country there have only been two instances where a convicted murderer has subsequently repeated his crime. So the number of people the amendment is attempting to catch is really quite insignificant.
As to the second portion of the amendment dealing with hijacking, the security precautions now in force, causing some inconvenience at airports, appear to be proving effective. Since they have been imposed there has not been a single hijacking incident in this country, and very few internationally. Therefore, I submit that the proposed amendment does nothing to increase public safety. Nevertheless, I agree with those who say the public are justifiably concerned about this issue because of the fear they have for their own safety. The difficulty is that capital punishment does nothing whatsoever to increase the safety of the Canadian people. Remember that as a society we originally decided to give up our right to defend ourselves as individuals. We gave up this right to another authority. It was in the nature of a bargain. We said: We will no longer defend ourselves; we will give that task to the police. At the same time we made a bargain with the police, and said: We shall obey the laws if you give us protection.
One of the causes for anxiety when we consider the rising crime rate is that every level of society has violated this bargain. Offenders range from the man who tries to beat a parking ticket to the man who flashes the lights of his car to tell others that a radar trap is ahead. The law has to apply to all of us, not just to some of us. This is something Spiro Agnew has just found out to his chagrin. It is for everybody. It is not "law for you, and I will give the orders." The great authority on law and order has been found with his hand in the cookie jar.

Capital punishment is not a solution. It is interesting to note the stages by which this debate developed into an emotional orgy in which members lost sight of reality. I am sorry the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) is not here. This is what he said in July about his decision to become an advocate of capital punishment. He said the case of Tanya Bush was the one which finally swung his opinion from abolition to retention. He said:
My friend, a learned criminal lawyer, fully knows the facts on Tanya Bush. They fit directly into the amendment of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin). Three child killings and then, while the culprit is out on weekend leave from a penitentiary, because he has a grudge against Tanya Bush's father, he kills Tanya Bush, who is eight or nine years old. Four child killings, three girls and one boy.
As I say, I wish the hon. member for Annapolis Valley were in the House today, because if he would examine the facts he would find that the murderer of Tanya Bush murdered only once. Yet I have received letters from people insisting that this man was repeatedly a murderer. No one will defend that kind of monstrous conduct. He was a dangerous sexual offender. With the kind of emo-

tional orgy we are engaging in we have lost all sense of logic and reason. I hope when the hon. member for Annapolis Valley finds out the real facts of the Tanya Bush case, the case that apparently convinced him to be an advocate of capital punishment, he will equally be persuaded to return to the sensible position that he once took, that of abolition.
The real facts are that capital punishment does not increase public safety; it reduces it. There is every reason to believe this. First of all, the kind of person who murders is one who often has a suicidal tendency. The question of penalty is immaterial; he may commit a murder in order to seek death.

From 16 years of experience. That is one instance where capital punishment reduces public safety. A second, and perhaps more important one, is the refusal of a jury to convict when they know that the death penalty will compound their error if they make one. Put a person in a dock for a week, then try to convince the jury over and over again that they must be certain beyond reasonable doubt of his guilt before taking the man's life, and the chances of his being released are much greater when there is a death penalty hanging over his head. Therefore, if you want to increase public safety you do not vote for capital punishment. Under capital punishment there is all sorts of evidence that the guilty go free.
Let me give the House another example. Let me go back to the Tanya Bush case to which the hon. member for Annapolis Valley referred some time ago. This was the case that convinced him to change his position. The evidence against the accused was circumstantial. There was evidence that two Crown witnesses changed their story. There was no eye witness to the crime. The chances of that man's being freed on the basis of the case they made out against him would have been much higher had capital punishment been hanging over him and the jury had to be sure within moral certainty that they would not take his life in error.

There is no doubt that if you are to sit in judgment on a man you are much more ready to send him to jail where a reasonable doubt exists than you are to take his life. Although the argument that the public are concerned is a valid one, the argument that capital punishment increases public safety simply will not wash.
I suggest we have to get back to respect for the rule of law. That means that we do not walk against a red light at Wellington and O'Connor. It means that we do not try to beat a parking ticket. It means that we do not speed. This principle must be adhered to by the whole of society. A society with a low crime rate is a society where laws are obeyed by every level of that society. One of the real problems in this country is that we are breaking society into sections and classes. Where advantage can be taken, it is being taken. It is just as wrong to beat the income tax as it is to beat your wife. You do not draw divisions on this

question. What we need to come back to is a cohesive society where we all obey the law, and capital punishment will not do anything to encourage that.
As far as increasing public safety is concerned, six million people in this country have a gun. Under the present law, any person, regardless of mental history, can walk into a store and buy a gun. He may very well have been beating his wife for the previous three weeks and have a paranoid delusion that she is about to kill him. There is no law to stop him purchasing a rifle. I suggest this is one area where we can make a positive contribution to public safety. The very minimum that we should require, surely, is that a person who wants to buy a gun should have a certificate of competence, that he be without a history of mental illness or criminal activity, and that he should be a person who knows something about the law relating to guns and their use. We do not have such a minimum standard in this country.
I rather agree with those in this House who have expressed their view that the majority of the people in this country favour retention of capital punishment. There is no point avoiding public opinion when it seems to be so obvious. Certainly, my mail reflects the fact that the majority of those in my riding favour retention of capital punishment. Mr. Speaker, in addressing ourselves to Bill C-2 and these amendments, once again before us, we realize that there are as many shades of opinion on the abolition or retention of capital punishment among members of this House as there are degrees in a compass. However, attention should be focused on the fact that there is a common link in both arguments. It is based on the fact that the compassion for human life is a basic, all-embracing tenet of western civilization, and thus the common concern in both arguments is the preservation of life itself.
Advocates of abolition, however, imply that a retention-ist is not concerned with life and that his argument in favour of the death penalty is a barbaric and uneducated one. Typical is a speech by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) who said:
The outcome of this debate will reveal the level of civilization, sophistication, compassion and understanding in Canadian society.
Thus, abolitionists would have those who argue for the retention of the death penalty feel that their view is a retrogressive one, not compatible with the temper of the times. Abolitionists would have those who argue in favour of the death penalty feel that they have only to wait and they will see the light.
From those intellectuals who are seized with the problems of the higher civilization, an occasional tear might be looked for over the savagely mutilated bodies of victims and their mentally ravaged kinfolk. There are those who say that corpses don't talk, but as Molly Lefevre pointed out in her book entitled "Evidence for the Crown", corpses talk. They talk of stupidity, depravity, perversion. They talk of crimes of every kind and they talk of easy living in pleasant homes, of hard lives, of joys that ended in sorrow, of tragedy and of broken hearts. That we are living in the super-civilized 20th century is indeed a fact. Unfortunately, the fellow with the gun does not seem to know one century from another.
It is one of the stock arguments of anti-capital punish-mentarians that the threat of the death penalty is an empty threat and frightens no would-be murderer. However, while arguments and statistics have been stacked on both sides of the balance, the deterrent effect of capital punishment remains unresolved. On these grounds, Mr. Speaker, I challenge the dogmatic assumptions of those who say the death penalty serves no purpose, as the statement has obvious imperfections.
The categorical assertion that "the death penalty serves no purpose" is contradicted by a number of self-evident facts. There is no shortage of reported instances wherein more than one homicide was committed by the same culprit, either as a result of not being apprehended on time

October 18, 1973
Capital Punishment
during an escape or after being erroneously acquitted. This being so, it is at least indisputable that a killer, once he has been liquidated, is forever incapable of killing again. Considered under this aspect alone, it would seem that the death penalty has in the past achieved at least one purpose.
With the passing of years, the character of the prison population is being increasingly tainted by a continual infusion of more belligerent inmates. It is perhaps the too-ready acceptance of the dogma that the death penalty serves no purpose that has helped to give rise to a situation in which the maintenance of discipline within prison walls is an increasing problem.
Under the morality of our time, severity in dealing with those guilty of bloodshed is stigmatized as revenge and this is looked upon as a greater crime, or at least as great as the motivating offence, but the alleged sinfulness of vengeance, revenge, or retribution-call it what you will- has never been established.
There are those who seem to think evil deeds ought to be resented, but not punished, or at least not punished to the extent of the death penalty, but should it be a wrong doctrine if we seek to impose it on those who will have none of it? To us, the legislators who urge that this moral precept be converted into an act of parliament, the following question could be asked: whose cheek is it that we are so ready to turn to the hand of the smiter? Is it your own cheek or those of the other people? Shall we admonish a distracted widow, crying out for the law's vengeance, there, there, now, you musn't be so vindictive.
Those opposed to the death penalty frequently argue that there is always the possibility of some innocent person being destroyed, either through malice or error, and that to avoid such tragedies, it is better that no one be executed. It should be pointed out, however, and this cannot be too strongly maintained, that there is not a single human enterprise or sphere of activity that is not marred at some time or another by a deplorable episode. Although much-is made of the comparatively remote possibility of some innocent person being put to death for a crime he did not commit, hardly any note is ever taken of the lethal aftermath that can follow an erroneous acquittal. It is a false and utterly unattainable idea of perfect justice and unerring accuracy. It would sacrifice a hundred real and present advantages to society through the permanent removal of men who are and can be at times really no better than noxious animals, thus obviating the possible infliction of wrong upon some unknown victim at some unknown future date. To insist that the execution of specific enemies be forbidden on humanitarian grounds makes neither moral nor political sense.
In an ideal society, war would not be one of the normal activities. Violence would not be one of the normal activities of even the smallest minority of its members and there would be neither need for prisons nor for punishment. It is not to crush optimism that I say there will never be a utopian society, but that being so, it is not necessarily the best policy to endeavour to approach its imagined conditions.
What is wanted is the best possible society, and there is no reason to assume, given the knowledge that such a society will contain and endorse violence, that the best

possible will exclude the death penalty. In fact, the Canadian people have indicated that they believe otherwise. Although here and there triumphant, the movement for the total abolition of the death penalty has by no means been greeted with universal acceptance.
If our parliamentary democracy is to respond to the people, our fellow Canadians have indicated-and we have heard numerous constituency polls cited in the House- that capital punishment should be reinstated. In the October 1972 Weekend Magazine poll of readers from urban and rural centres, some 30,139 indicated that retention is necessary compared to 3,383 who think it is not. In April 1966, 255 people voted in this House in favour of the retention of capital punishment. However, in 1967, Bill C-168, introduced by Solicitor General Pennel to confine for an experimental period of five years the possible imposition of the death penalty to the murder of police officers and prison guards while on duty, was passed by a reasonably comfortable majority.
On July 4, 1972, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), then Solicitor General, said:
It is difficult in the present situation to make an accurate assessment of the five year trial period since it has not ended.
He added that the required statistics which would make retrospective analysis possible would not be available until one more year had lapsed.
The year has now lapsed, the July date has come and gone and again we find before us a request for the introduction of a five-year ban on capital punishment. We find ourselves once again at square one because this government circumvented the will of Parliament by commuting death sentences in cases to which capital punishment still applied, and which in normal circumstances would not justify the exercise of the prerogative of mercy. Because it is a question so fundamental, it is the last of issues upon which a nation's leaders should abdicate, as has been the case.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the amendment before us which proposes that this bill be amended to provide for capital punishment in the instance where a person already convicted of murder commits a second murder, and in the instance where someone has been found guilty of air piracy or as it is sometimes called skyjacking, I do so because I feel there are certain matters which perhaps are not properly understood by certain members of this House.
Surely, the question of the abolition of capital punishment or its retention is something on which the government in power has a responsibility to take a stand. We see in this instance that the government has chosen not to stand up and be counted, but indirectly to give the impression that there is a free vote in this House. It is granted, Mr. Speaker, that there is to be a free vote in the technical sense, but I suggest when the vote is taken later this evening concerning the amendment before us we will see the whip will be present and that, for example, every member of the cabinet will vote against this amendment. Surely, if members of the cabinet are so uniform in their
October 18, 1973

view in respect of the amendment and the bill itself, they should have the courage to endorse this measure as a government measure.
I mention this because I feel perhaps their handling of this legislation, including the unfortunate performance by its sponsor during the committee hearings, is so typical of the government's mishandling of matters generally. I see, for example, that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) graces the chamber today. Surely, there is no other department which more clearly illustrates the lack of foresight of this government than his department. Here we are situated with a minister who, because of lack of foresight, is jumping from country to country and from province to province in an effort to solve various problems which he should have been solving months and even years ago.
To come back to the question of capital punishment, I mentioned lack of foresight because I sincerely believe that in respect of capital punishment this government again is out of step with the world. Others in the world know there is an energy crisis. It was foreseen five or ten years ago. Many governments took steps to minimize its effect, but not our government. In the case of capital punishment, we know that the world, rather than going abolitionist at the present time, is actually becoming more retentionist. Yet we find an instance here where the government indirectly-and I emphasize that-is attempting to bring in an abolitionist measure which it does not have the courage to sponsor. In doing so, it is out of step with the main trend in the world. Our honourable friends to the left have said, "Where?"
Most of us have heard of the United Nations. I think most of us have great respect for that body. I believe it would be interesting to read a current publication put out by the United Nations which indicates, contrary to the public view which people like to express, especially the academics, that the world in fact is not becoming more and more abolitionist.

Surely, those who propose to vote for abolition should ask themselves whether they truly believe that there is no crime so heinous that it does not warrant the supreme punishment, that is the loss of one's life. I would like each of those members, when they ask themselves that question, to read the gruesome details of, for example, the candy store murders which were recently in the public news in the United States. The fact that one or more persons systematically murdered relatively young people, had their bodies mutilated and buried, numbering as many as 20 at a time, indicates that although we may wish to do away with capital punishment, although we think that it is a desirable goal to never be put in a

situation of having to take another person's life in the name of the state, we would be wise to ask ourselves how we in this country would react if such a heinous crime occurred here. Is that not at least one case where the convicted person who is responsible for this crime should be asked to pay the supreme penalty, that is the loss of his life?
Having said that, I feel that it is important that we bear in mind that one of the most heinous crimes is that of air piracy where a person, for reasons of his own, is willing to murder the occupants of an aeroplane. There is little imaginable that could be worse than that type of activity. That is the partial effect of the amendment that is before us. It proposes that capital punishment be applied in the event of murder connected with skyjacking. I think it is important, in view of the general trend noted by the United Nations which is not toward abolition but toward retention of capital punishment, that we in this country make sure that Canada does not become a haven for those who conduct skyjackings in any place in the world.

I say that the laws will toughen up on this subject worldwide, and it is not the time for this incompetent government to be taking Canada in exactly the opposite direction to the general trend in the world.
If I may conclude my comments on this amendment, I will simply refer to a statement made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). On July 23, as recorded at page 5902 of Hansard, he asked:
How in God's name does one help the victim of help the family by hanging the murderer?
With all due respect, I suggest that that is not the question. It is quite true that neither the victim nor the family is aided by capital punishment, but it is not the purpose of capital punishment to do so. The state ought not to be concerned with providing retribution for the victim. The punishment is given because the murderer has broken the law. Punishment is a transaction between the offending individual and the state, in which no one ought to interfere and which should be carried out by the state solely with reference to its own laws which have been broken and without reference to anything extraneous to that fact.
I suggest that the Solicitor General's question obscures the distinction between why one punishes a person because he has broken the law and what purpose the punishment is intended to serve, that is, deterrence, reformation or some other reason. I believe the victim or family ought never to enter into the consideration with respect to punishment. Were they to so enter, what argument could the Solicitor General provide to prevent one from applying his question to all forms of punishment? It could be asked: How in God's name does one help the victim or help the family by jailing the criminally negligent drunken driver? Punishment surely is not handed out for the benefit of certain individuals. It is the action of a state for the general benefit of its members. I believe the Solicitor General obscured this fact when he asked how it helps the family or the victim. That, I repeat, is not the question.

We need laws in this country. We need stronger laws to deal with some of the criminal activity in this country. It is up to the government in power at the time to introduce those stronger laws and to see that the penalty, be it the death penalty or otherwise, is executed. In that connection I would suggest that the present government, perhaps more than any government since confederation, has brought our legal system into disrespect through its commutation of death sentences without exception.
I see that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker. I simply conclude by urging hon. members, before they vote on this matter, to give it serious second thought if they choose to vote against the motion proposed by my hon. colleague, because I believe that by voting in an abolitionist way we are in fact going against the world trend, and I know we are going against public opinion in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so far I have not spoken at any stage of this debate except in committee, and then only with respect to details of the bill and not on the fundamental question that we are being asked to deal with here. At this stage of our proceedings I do not expect that anything I say will overly influence anybody one way or another, either on the amendments or on the bill itself at third reading, but I feel it necessary to express my feelings on the subject as I have done in previous parliaments.
First, I think there was an element of extreme weakness on the part of the government in taking the course that it did; in other words, trying to have it both ways. I wish the bill before us were absolute in one direction or another so that it either proposed to endorse the concept of capital punishment for all murders, or proposed not to have capital punishment for any murders. In that way parliament could give a clear response to it.
It is to be regretted that the government, which was in office last year, knowing the five-year experimental period was coming to an end, sought to play a little political game and hide from the five-year termination period with the hope that the October election would return the Liberal Party with a comfortable majority so that this year it could do as it saw fit with respect to capital punishment. But that did not happen. In any event, we are now faced with this bill.
I do not favour the concept of capital punishment. I never have. I look upon this bill as posing a difficult question to hon. members, because to vote for it now and on third reading is to vote for capital punishment in a limited way, and to vote against it is also to vote for capital punishment in a limited way. Either way, yes or no, parliament is endorsing in a limited manner the concept of capital punishment. That is why I wish the government had been more determined in its approach and had proposed a bill clearly one way or the other. But it did not.
We can look at the question of murder and of capital punishment in relation thereto from the point of view of capital punishment being a deterrent, or from the point of view of it being the state responding in a vengeful manner to the taking of life. I, for one, cannot condone the idea or concept that the state-meaning the entire nation, the country, the government and parliament-can possibly think in terms of revenge. I cannot believe that the state
Capital Punishment
can possibly adjust its thinking in a mass way to say: We are going to reflect the view of the injured party and wreak vengeance on the person who committed the offence of murder.
I think, with respect to what the state is, the nation is and the government and parliament are supposed to be, that we have to think in terms of the potential of a deterrent. Is the threat of criminal law sanction sufficient to deter a person from committing a particular crime? That is the way I try to look at it and that is the way I feel about it. I do not believe the threat of capital punishment is any more a deterrent to the commission of the crime of murder than is the threat of a long jail sentence-neither any more nor any less.
While we are on the subject, Mr. Speaker, let me point out that the law for the past five years has said that a person convicted of murdering a police officer while on duty, or a prison guard, shall be subjected to capital punishment. As much as I abhor the concept of capital punishment and think it is not a deterrent, as long as that provision was on the statute books then those people convicted under it should have been hanged. The government had no right whatever, and either did its predecessor nor the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) when he was prime minister, to avoid a law passed by parliament by the use of the royal prerogative of mercy. If parliament passed a law to the effect that if you murder a policeman while he is on duty, are convicted and sentenced to hang, then you should be hanged, much as I detest that concept. The law should not be brought into disrepute by an action of government.
I am as sure as I am standing here, knowing the position of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield)-he has declared it and he is an honourable man-that if he became prime minister, regardless of the speeches made by members who want to retain the death penalty, he would exercise this so-called royal prerogative and commute the death sentence. He has said he would do that. Is that flying in the face of the potential law any more than the present government is? No. It is the same situation. I have the view that when parliament passes a law it should expect it to be carried out, not subverted, not distorted, not put to one side.
If we want, as a parliament, to declare that there shall be no capital punishment, then we should do so. However, we should not be hypocritical and say we are going to vote for or against a bill knowing full well that nobody is going to be hanged because of the declarations on the matter by people in responsible positions. But, Mr. Speaker, that is aside from the general question.
Let us look at some circumstances, Mr. Speaker. This is the way in which I tend to relate my feelings about whether the threat of capital punishment is a stronger deterrent than is the threat of life imprisonment. If we look at the emotions of human beings, we see that these are inflamed or distorted or advanced as a result of family quarrels, lovers quarrels or mix-ups in family life. We see that they are inflamed or distorted as a result of excessive drinking, whether it be in a tavern or a home. We see that the emotions are anaesthestized by alcohol or some other

chemical and perhaps a murder takes place. We are entitled to ask ourselves if the threat of capital punishment would deter a person, under these circumstances, from committing murder. It would not be a deterrent, it would not even be a factor in a person's thinking.
If two individuals get into a squabble after sitting in a tavern all night and retire outside to settle their differences in a physical way during which one kills the other, he has not considered the possibility of the death penalty. It was not a factor in his thinking at all. An emotional disturbance in a home, a shooting as a result of all night drinking or a reflection of what poverty does to a family, are not factors when it comes to the question of murder.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) referred to rape. I suppose, but I do not know, nor I am sure does any other member of this House know from personal experience, that in the process of an act of rape the emotions of the aggressor are so distorted, inflamed and out of touch with reality, that that person is not thinking about the threat of capital punishment or any other kind of punishment but is influenced by the immediacy of the situation.
Let us put it in reverse. I do not like to do this in any unkind way to the hon. member for Louis-Hebert but I think her amendment distorts the relationship between man and woman, because it speaks in terms of a male person committing rape upon a female person. The reverse is true, Mr. Speaker; the reverse circumstances have happened. I know of an instance some years ago where a woman forced a man at gunpoint to perform the act of cunnilingus on her. That is rape. It is not rape in the pure legal sense which, as I understand it, is a penetration of the vagina by the penis. It is not that kind of rape but it is certainly forcing an individual to perform a sexual act. The hon. member for Louis-Hebert did not take that into account obviously, but it is a fact of human behaviour.

speechtext:
My smart-assed friend says she has not been around as I have. Mr. Speaker, I am trying to speak on a matter that is pretty serious and not reflect upon comments anyone else has made during this debate. If the hon. member wants to make that comment during the course of a speech, all right. He may have done so, already, but let us not cast aspersions against the feelings that one individual has about something.
What I am trying to get at, Mr. Speaker, is that the amendment on the question of rape referred to a highly emotional situation. I submit that the threat of capital punishment or a life sentence would not have any relevance whatsoever in the circumstances. Even a person about to commit a bank robbery or some other kind of criminal offence is not thinking of the threat of capital punishment or of a life sentence. The criminal mind says "I have looked at all the circumstances. I can perform this robbery and if in the course of it I am about to be apprehended by a policeman and I shoot him, I can get away with it. They are not going to catch me".
The criminal sets out a careful plan for avoiding apprehension. He looks at the possibility of a life sentence but feels he is going to get away with the bank robbery because he has laid it out carefully. In the city of Mont-

real, the criminals have bank robbery almost down to a science and have it timed to a minute and 15 seconds or something. The bank robbery is laid out so carefully that the robbers know it takes a certain number of seconds from the time they get into the bank until the police get there-unless the police happen to be just around the corner. It is a carefully laid plan, and the threat of capital punishment or a life sentence is not a deterrent to the commission of the crime.
The psychotic, the person completely out of touch with reality, the dangerous sexual offender, the person who attacks another and cuts him in pieces, who buries him alive or performs some obscenities on the body or commits all sorts of atrocities-that person is not considering the threat of capital punishment. I do not know what factors such persons consider, and I do not know whether, even psychiatrists know, but the threat of capital punishment is not any more of a deterrent than any other form of punishment that carries with it some strong sanction, such as life imprisonment.
I can think of one set of circumstances in which the threat of capital punishment might be a deterrent. That is the case of an individual who has been sentenced to imprisonment for life, which means 20 to 25 years. The death penalty might be a deterrent in that instance because he can only receive one life sentence; he can only spend the rest of his life in jail. Perhaps in that situation the possibility of losing his life might be a deterrent to committing murder.
On the other hand, depending upon the individual, it might be attractive to commit murder. Talk to people who are in jail, people who are subject to sentences of 45 or 50 years. Talk to people who have been sentenced to life imprisonment because they have committed murder. Talk to them about a life-term jail sentence. They say; "I would just as soon be dead as face the prospect of life in jail." So this person might ask: What have I got to live for? And if I die, I might as well take one of those screws-prison guards-or one of those finks or informers with me.
I cannot myself think of picking and choosing instances and circumstances and saying to myself, guided by my own conscience, yes, it is all right to impose capital punishment in circumstance (a) but not in circumstances (b) or in circumstance (c). Yet this what we are seeking to do in the bill before us. This is what the minister was seeking to do when he introduced this bill. He was saying it was acceptable to impose capital punishment in two sets of circumstances but not in others. And in my view he picked the two that are meaningless, the two which have no consequence.
Is there a world trend in this regard? Does it matter to the conscience of people here whether or not Great Britain retains or does not retain capital punishment? Does it matter whether Iceland does or does not retain capital punishment? Capital punishment might be in force there one week, and the next week it might not. Attitudes throughout the world, in every jurisdiction are subject to change. Attempts have been made to deal with the question of criminality, to deal with the question of taking of life. All it proves to me, both from a logical and a statisti-
October 18, 1973

cal point of view, is that in every jurisdiction where an attempt has been made to use capital punishment as a deterrent to murder, they cannot prove it has succeeded. And in every jurisdiction where capital punishment has been avoided, they cannot show success either. In other words, it is a draw. In other words, no great deterrent to murder is achieved by the threat or imposition of capital punishment.
I had the idea that I might discuss the question of unrest in prisons, a point touched upon by one of the earlier speakers. I think, now, I shall not do so. It is beside the point. There is a reason for it, but the situation can be dealt with without the threat of imposition of capital punishment. The problem of the anger and unrest in prisons can be dealt with by a little straightening out in the department itself.
I know we all have a tendency in certain circumstances, at the moment of a heinous crime, at the instant of an atrocity against a person, to look at the circumstances and say, "My God, isn't that terrible? That person should be hanged."

Mr. Speaker, having spoken at length on the principle of this bill on second reading, I shall refer only at this time to the amendment put forward by the hon. member for North-umberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence). That hon. member has offered two amendments in one package for our consideration. In one part of the package he suggests that a person be subject to capital punishment if he causes the death of a human being after having been previously
Capital Punishment
convicted of murder. In the second he suggests a person be convicted of capital murder if he commits murder in conjunction with a hijacking. The wording of the second part of the amendment uses the following terminology:
. . . any person, where such person causes the death of a human being and has been previously convicted of murder, whether or not such murder is punishable by death . . .
With all due respect, I point out that the situation envisioned by the hon. member is an extremely rare occurrence. The commonly held view of the average murderer as being one who either repeats his crime or commits other crimes is simply erroneous. The recidivism rate of murderers is among the lowest of all types of crime. Indeed, in the entire history of Canada there have been only three individuals who have ever been convicted a second time of murder. That being the case, I feel the amendment suggested by the hon. member seeks to effect a cure for a disease which is so rare as to be almost non-existent.
It is also conceivable that a case could arise where a person falling under the provisions of the amendment would have been guilty of a first murder which was considered much more heinous than the second murder. As a matter of fact, the second event might not even be a case of capital murder at all in terms of the present law. According to the hon. member's wording, he says "where such person causes the death of a human being". I suggest that that wording is very bad from the legal point of view, but I presume that according to that wording a person could be convicted of capital murder after having committed manslaughter in the second instance, or having committed non-culpable homicide according to the terms of the present law. Yet he would be executed because of the second event. I do not use the word "murder" because the hon. member who put forward the amendment did not use that term either.
With respect to the second amendment which deals with skyjacking, the hon. member seeks to extend capital punishment to the case of, again using his words, such person who "causes the death of a human being"-again he uses those words instead of "commits culpable homicide", or something to that effect-"while committing or attempting to commit an offence under section 76.1 of the Criminal Code." Section 76.1 deals with hijacking.
Before getting into the entire hijacking question, I suggest that from a legal point of view merely to say "causes the death of a human being" without defining the type of murder or offence is not satisfactory.
With regard to aircraft hijacking, I agree that this subject has sparked considerable debate throughout the world. The fact that all nations consider aircraft hijacking to be a severe threat is reflected in the fact that many nations, including Canada, have moved to take strong action to prevent such incidents from occurring. For example, in Canada in recent years we have had amendments to the Criminal Code and the Aeronautics Act; within the RCMP we have set up special constables to deal with airport security, and we have mandatory checks made to prevent hijacking. So, we have taken considerable steps to try to prevent hijacking or terrorism on aircraft.

As a further expression of this concern, the amendment offered by the hon. member is certainly understandable. However, I would argue that the benefits that may at first glance seem to accrue from this amendment are illusory. Perhaps the main objection to this amendment on purely legal grounds is the difficulty of interpretation that might ensue.
Another argument that I feel offers sufficient grounds for rejecting the amendment arises from a consideration of the very different circumstances in which hijacking has taken place. I have in mind recent examples where the hijacker was very disturbed and the hijacking was almost entirely the product of his mental disturbance, although his mental state was not such as to make him unfit to stand trial. If by some mischance his action had caused death, it would not seem that his case should be one to which the death penalty should be automatically applied. James A. Arey, who has written a very detailed book on the subject of skyjacking, offers us his opinion that skyjackers fall into five major categories, which he defines as, first, losers and misfits; second, emotional disaster cases; third, criminals on the run; fourth, individuals with personal, political reasons, and fifth, people or groups with organized political motivations.
With specific respect to hijacking, I feel it vital to emphasize again that it is the almost unanimous consensus of the experts that hijackers are best deterred by preventing them from getting on an aircraft in the first place. That is the best deterrent to the hijacker and the best prevention of the problems he may cause.
In the past year, as hon. members will recall, elaborate ground security installations have been made in airports across Canada and the United States, as well as Europe. I think it should suffice to say that since those security checks were begun there has been only one Canadian hijacking: the attempt by a man to divert a Quebecair flight from its scheduled Wabush to Montreal run on December 14 last. Before those measures were introduced there were seven hijackings over Canadian territory. Mr. Ted Abrams of the International Civil Aviation Organization in Montreal was quoted as saying that "1973 was a good year" with respect to hijacking. He said that hijackings have decreased mightly around the globe. And a Federal Aviation Administration spokesman in Washington, D.C. confirmed that since January 5, when the FAA made pre-flight security checks mandatory for all passengers and baggage, there have been no hijackings of U.S. planes.
In the light of these facts, I think it is fair to say that the amendment offered by the hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham is again a case of much too much too late. The problem of hijacking appears to have been controlled by much less severe measures than those which he advocates. Furthermore, the usefulness of a death penalty in connection with hijacking offences is seriously questioned by experts in the field. Mr. Arey, in summing up the opinions of experts with respect to this problem, finds "general agreement in regard to a multilevel approach." He suggests that a consensus can be found concerning the following important points:

The act of skyjacking must be recognized as a crime by all aviation bodies and all governments; severe punishment should be swift and inevitable.
I stress the next sentence of Mr. Arey's conclusion most emphatically:
Punishment should not include the death sentence, because that penalty is unlikely to have any effect on extremely unbalanced or desperate individuals. It should consist of long incarceration in a prison or a mental institution. Sentences should be made as uniform as possible throughout the world.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I call upon hon. members to heed the words of experts in the field, experts who feel that the death sentence would simply have no effect on the sort of person who engages in the crime of hijacking in the first place. In view of the fact that some of the skyjackers are severely unbalanced individuals bent on suicide, a death penalty may actually serve as incentive to the commission of the crime.
With these arguments in mind, I feel that an overwhelming case can be made that the suggestions offered by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, while offered for our consideration with the best of intentions, simply cannot stand up to examination on legal, psychological, or statistical grounds. I stress again that these arguments can be made against the amendment irrespective of one's view on the general question of capital punishment.
Before I close I should like to respond to a few of the remarks made earlier this day in the debate on these amendments. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) was quoting from a document which pointed out that there were only nine countries in the world that have completely abolished capital punishment. I think that is probably true if it applies to all crimes; but if he considers the complete abolition of capital punishment for cases of murder, which is what we are considering in this House, then he will find that there are many more than nine countries. For example, the United Kingdom has completely abolished capital punishment for murder but not for treason, and this is why it is not included in the group of countries that he put forward. Many of the states of the United States have completely abolished capital punishment for murder, but in the United States generally they have capital punishment for treason and perhaps other offences, very rare offences, against the state.
In Canada, with this bill, we are only considering capital punishment for murder. Whether the bill is carried, or defeated, we will not touch upon the question of capital punishment for treason which exists under another section of our Code, or the old crime of piracy which also still exists: it is sort of an anachronism in our law, but it still exists.
In quoting the cases, I think the hon. member may have misled the House to a certain extent. The important question is, how many countries have completely abolished capital punishment for the crime of murder? He also referred to my statement in which I asked, "How in God's name does it help the victim or the family of the victim if we maintain capital punishment?" In stating that, I was merely replying to some arguments of members of this House who suggested it was helpful to the family of the
October 18, 1973

victim and maybe to the victim himself. That is why I phrased my reply in that way. That certainly is not my principal argument on the question of capital punishment.
The hon. member also wanted to know why we had not taken a position as a government. The bill before the House is a government bill; it was put forward by the cabinet. Under our constitution, the cabinet is legally the government. This is a cabinet bill, approved by cabinet. In that sense it is the same as the bill put forward in 1967. However, it is different from the motion of 1966 which was put forward by four private members of this House. In all cases there was a free vote, but in 1966 there was not a government bill. In 1967 there was a government bill. This is a government bill. For the members of our party and all other parties, as far as we are concerned it is a free vote, but not for the government, meaning the cabinet. This is a cabinet, government bill. Cabinet discussed this question and we decided to put forward this bill. I put it forward on behalf of the government.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) referred to the amendments I attempted to put forward in committee. They referred to that as contempt of parliament. In one other case the hon. member suggested that it was unethical. There is nothing in our rules to suggest amendments cannot be put forward either in committee of the whole House or in one of our special or standing committees. As a matter of fact it has been done many times, not only by members of the opposition but by members of the government and its ministers.
If I remember correctly, during the tax reform bill several amendments were put forward by the government. The hon. member for Edmonton West did not complain at that time. No one has complained about the other amendment I put forward in committee, the one to restrict the parole eligibility provisions for murderers. If members are against the principle of ministers putting forth amendments in committee, they should object to that amendment as well. They object to the amendment they do not like, but not to the one they like. It has not even been mentioned in this debate.
