Mr. Speaker, there is quite a difference between nine and 23, but the fact is this: I do not have the list before me, but I know that in western Europe, where most of the people of this country originate from, only three countries have not completely abolished capital punishment for murder. Many of them have it for other crimes. The three countries are Ireland, France and Spain. Africa, Asia and many communist states have capital punishment for many crimes. In South Africa they hang people by the dozen from month to month; but I do not think we should emulate that country.
I wish to refer to some of the remarks of the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn). He said we must support the amendment of the hon. member for Northumberland Durham (Mr. Lawrence) because the government had not done anything to deal with the question of security in penitentiaries, and that murderers were escaping on a large scale. I wish to point out that since the rash of escapes in April and May-one of which was an escaped murderer-namely, in June, July, August and September we had a 75 per cent decrease in escapes from Canadian penitentiaries in comparison with the year before. This is because we took very serious measures to deal with the problem of security. We increased the number of guards, the perimeter of security by erecting extra fencing, and so on. We have dealt with that problem. If that is the reason the hon. member is supporting the amendment, it is not very good because we have already taken steps. I regret we had to do that, but it was necessary.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said he supports the bill. I thank him for his support. He made some points in his speech with which I should deal. He referred to answers I made today in the House in which I said we were looking for new penitentiary space in British Columbia. He thought that was a very bad move. In the penitentiary at New Westminster, B.C., there were approximately 630 inmates last week. This is in a penitentiary that is supposed to hold approximately 550. It is a maximum security prison. The hon. member seemed to imply that we should put these maximum security inmates on parole. He blamed the cutback in parole on the chairman of the parole board. I should point out that under the present chairman paroles reached an all-time high in 1970. They increased at a very extensive rate between 1965 and 1970. However, after 1970 they found there was a very high rate of violation. The people who are back in penitentiary are for the most part there as a result of violation of parole.
Over the 14-year period the parole board has been in operation, the failure rate has been about 20 per cent. However, last year it was 56 per cent. We are very concerned about that failure rate, as is the chairman of the parole board. He is re-examining the position he took in 1968, 1969 and 1970 to try to see what went wrong during those years in order to correct some of these matters. In the meantime we are faced with a situation in British Columbia where the prison population last year increased by more than 14 per cent when the usual increase is only 4 per cent. Many of these people are maximum security risks. We cannot place them on parole. We must find institutions in which to put them. That is what we are trying to do. I think I have dealt with some of the remarks made in the debate. I suggest again to the House that the

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA

speechtext:
The House resumed, from Monday, April 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-164, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways System and Air Canada for the period from the 1st day of January, 1973, to the 30th day of June, 1974, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain

securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the CNR financing bill has appeared on the order paper for several years, and for reasons that need not be repeated since most members are aware of them, it has yet to be called and passed. Now during that period, it has been impossible to submit to the consideration of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications the annual reports of the CNR as well as those of Air Canada, because under the law, before being tabled in the House, those reports must be audited by firms of accountants recognized throughout Canada. Now, precisely on that point the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance who introduced the bill in April 1973 mentioned that it might be advisable to make some changes in the appointment of auditors. I think that the first change that we should make-and I am pleased to see here the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) responsible for the bill-would be to delete in the legislation the provision requiring Parliament to appoint the auditors of the books of the CNR and Air Canada.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that among all Crown corporations that come directly or indirectly under the federal government, this is the only case where Parliament has to appoint a firm of auditors in order to have these two corporations' books audited in an efficient way.
In my opinion, the first change that should be made would be to remove from Parliament the responsibility for appointing auditing firms in order to let private enterprise and other firms of auditors the opportunity to enter into competition with the auditors appointed by Parliament.
If we go back several years, we notice an anomaly: the auditors appointed to audit these corporations' books were always employed by English firms, which means that there was never an opportunity for a French firm to get the auditing contract for the CNR or Air Canada.
I think that this is an anomaly that should be straightened out as early as possible because we certainly cannot by an act of Parliament rule out the possibility that qualified French firms, which have expanded in this country, might compete with these two firms.
As I said earlier, the fact that Parliament has to appoint auditors is delaying the procedures of the Transportation committee, including consideration of the annual reports of these two firms, and I believe that passing of this legislation is urgent. By my action tonight, I certainly do not intend to delay referral of the bill to the committee, which should take place at the earliest opportunity, but rather to point out that this bill contains an anomaly which should be straightened out as soon as possible.
Let us now take the examples of some Crown corporations, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Industrial Development Bank, to name only two. We note that the auditors are appointed alternately, as suggested by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Comtois), but the alternance is based on bilingualism, in that an English-speaking firm alternates
October 18, 1973

with a French-speaking one, which means that those firms which have reached a certain level of maturity and importance in respect of their personnel may hope to obtain contracts for auditing the accounts of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the Industrial Development Bank or the Bank of Canada, which is not the case for two large corporations, namely the CNR and Air Canada.
I should like to deal also with the competition on the commercial routes of the CNR. As it had done many times before, the Canadian Trucking Association and the Quebec Trucking Association have stated recently that because there is no separate accounting for the money received by the federal government and the CN and that paid within their own operations, it is very difficult to determine whether the federal government is now advancing money to help competition against private enterprise. If such were the case, I believe that it would constitute another injustice to be rectified.
If you refer to the 1972 Canadian National Railways annual report under consolidated income statement, you will note that the net revenue of separately operated trucking companies amounted to $1,766,180 in 1971 and $2,464,306 in 1972, which means that at the present time, the CN are competing more and more against private trucking companies which are not subsidized by the federal government. For instance, I believe that we should perhaps obtain figures showing how the National Railways spend the subsidies which they receive, and if these subsidies are used to promote competition with private businesses, we should rectify this failing of the legislation and propose an amendment. Obviously, this amendment should be submitted by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) when the bill concerning the Canadian National Railways is studied, and not in relation with financing. Such amendment should be submitted in order to stop this organization from having trucking activities and, consequently, to prevent it from competing against private enterprise.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have risen to speak on this particular CNR financing bill. I have reviewed the debate that has taken place on it, going back to last April when it first came before the House, and so far as I can gather an adequate explanation has not been given, to the House and the country, on the need for this bill, or of how the CNR and Air Canada operated without a financing bill being passed by the House of Commons for over two years.
At one time we were presented with Bill C-4, dealing with loans and expenditures with respect to CNR and Air Canada, for the period January 1, 1971, to June 30, 1972. It was not passed by the House, yet both companies managed to continue their operations. Now, we have Bill C-164 which deals with CNR financing from January 1, 1973, to June 30, 1974. What has happened to the intervening six months from June 30, 1972, to January 1, 1973? What is the explanation for that gap? How did the CN and Air Canada finance their operations during that period? I suppose
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada there is an adequate answer, and members of parliament are entitled to the explanation.
There is a further question with regard to the audited statement of the companies. Ever since I first came to the House of Commons, the annual reports of the CNR and Air Canada have been referred to the Standing Committee on Transportation. Now, the story is that the annual report was tabled but the auditors have not been assigned. The Auditor General, because of some mix-up at the time of the change over, brought about to satisfy the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) -

speechtext:
I am just asking for an explanation of this. The government switched the auditors. The Auditor General has not examined the CNR statement, so it is not an officially audited statement. Yet, it has been laid before the House without any full explanation.
Now, we have Bill C-164 before us, providing for capital expenditures of $75 million, including $8 million for branch lines. We want to examine the details of that $8 million for branch lines. In western Canada we are continually told that branch lines are to be abandoned, but here we find $8 million allocated for construction of branch lines. Then, there is the provision of $167 million for new equipment and $140 million for Air Canada. These expenditures have not been fully explained in the debate to date.
When parliament was called back to settle the railway dispute the Minister of Transport made a great speech about labour trouble. It was a very emotional pitch. He referred several times to blackmail being threatened. Blackmail is not a very common or polite word, but certainly political pressure was placed on the government for eight weeks and it failed to act quickly to settle that strike. As a result, the revenues lost to the railroads were greater than would have been the case had parliament been convened earlier, or had a suitable settlement been reached prior to that. I only hope that judge Hall, in his review of the matter, will find a settlement satisfactory to both parties.
When we talk about CNR financing, we are often told about the heavy burden of debt, that nobody has yet lifted from the back of the CNR. We are repeatedly told that it is an old debt, the debt incurred in the building of the defunct railroad which were taken over by Canadian National in the period 1917 to 1922. The fear is that this debt is too great a burden for the CNR to carry, and that is why they have to come to parliament for financial assistance from time to time and why the final accounts are in the red.
This thought, I believe was best expressed by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) on April 16, 1973, as recorded at page 3353 of Hansard:
Under successive old style governments it has been a tradition since 1923 to establish a public corporation to which they pay lip service and then refuse to let it function as it can and should. They handicap it with a debt structure that makes it impossible for it to succeed in any meaningful way . ..
7018

October 18, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
He goes on to suggest that this debt was incurred in the building of the Grand Trunk Railway and, as a result of the union of the Grand Trunk with the Pacific Railway and so on. If one stopped in the middle of the sentence in which he referred to the debt structure, one might think he comes very close to Social Credit thinking that group always accused the old style governments of operating in a debt structured economy. What he was really referring to, however, was the burden of debt incurred by the CNR during the early years of settlement in western Canada between 1917 and 1922.
What was the amount of that debt and where is it now? In 1936, the debt of the CNR stood at $2,435 million. The Dominion of Canada reduced that debt by roughly half to $1,184 million. That is the outstanding long-term debt brought about by the creation of the CNR. In 1951, the House of Commons passed the National Railway Revision Act, and the long-term funded debt of the company was again cut in half. I am rounding off these figures, Mr. Speaker. In 1951, the long-term outstanding debt of the CNR was cut from $1,472 million to $615 million. Then, that amount was further reduced by another $121 million.
Accepting the long-term debt of the CNR in 1951 as $615 million, we must still ask why it is as large as it is today. What is the problem? Shortly after Donald Gordon took over, he brought in what was called the complete dieselization of the Canadian National Railways. That was embarked upon in 1950-51 and cost the CNR $630 million, more than the long-term debt at that time. Mr. Speaker, any efficient business should be able to pay off its own capitalization, and it is important that this fact be pointed out so that we realize it is not necessarily the long-term outstanding debt of the CNR that causes it to finance as it does.
When Mr. Gordon took over the CNR in 1950, he complained about the outstanding debt until he got the House of Commons to reduce it by more than one-half, but as he pointed out succinctly at that time, much of this indebtedness arose out of bad bookkeeping. That may be so, but what are the bookkeeping practices of the CNR today? A close examination of the ledger would show how it is done.
When the dieselization program was inaugurated, many steam engines had been purchased and some had only served 10 years but were being amortized over nearly 40 years. Naturally, when they were retired after only ten years the bookkeeping debt against them was quite large. Mr. Gordon revamped the bookkeeping system of the CNR. He did not want the same thing to happen to the diesel engines, so they were amortized for one-third of their expected life of 35 years. Amortizing the purchase of machinery over one-third of its life expectancy makes the bookkeeping and the debt look very bad. One could almost call it creative bookkeeping and, in effect, that is what it is. The CNR financing system is programmed to show a gross national revenue of a little over $1 billion. By the time expenses are deducted, the revenue will exceed the operating expenses, but along comes a $42 million interest on debt and that puts the company in the red. They do not mind being in the red because the federal government picks up the tab.
I do not necessarily say this should not be so, but I do say that it was to Mr. Gordon's advantage to bring in a

creative bookkeeping system. It did not bother him to do that because he knew if he painted the picture in the red the government would pick up the tab. That is part of the motivation and it should be understood. The men charged with the operation of the CNR were motivated to conduct the bookkeeping that way because of the lesson learned in having to scrap the many useful steam engines and the heavy expenditures caused by dieselization.
I think we are coming to the point in our society where many people are suggesting that governments can run things as well as private enterprise. That feeling is apparent in some of the socialist provinces. Somewhere along the line we have to look at that picture and decide whether it is true.
It is interesting to note that in Kenneth Galbraith's book on the new industrial state he makes the statement that in the western world, the United States and Canada, highly skilled executive types have been developed and that they probably work just as hard for a government as for private enterprise because they feel that they can thus maintain their stature as the elite of executive management. This is not borne out when one studies the other great railroading problem of recent times, the wreck of the Penn Central. This company was the result of a combination of two great railroads in the United States, the New York Central and the Pennsylvania Railroad. All the facts were fed into a computer and it took ten years to make the decision that those two railroads should work well together. They complement each other. Why, then, did Penn Central go bankrupt shortly afterwards? It was because the personalities managing the two railways were not compatible. The trackage may have been, but the personalities were not. It is still people who in the end decide what will happen-people and what motivates them. Some of the brilliant men on the one railroad would not co-operate with those on the other.
In Canada, in 1967, the National Transportation Act was passed, designed by people who thought they had the answer. It was, indeed, a common notion in Canada, Britain and a number of other countries that if we could simply free the railroads from controls of one kind or another they would become competitive with other forms of transport and all would be well. Since 1967, the railroads have been given a great deal of freedom. Ask the minister a question about freight rates or schedules and he replies by saying the matter is out of his hands; parliament has passed the legislation and all he can do is ask the companies about it. It seems the idea of competition will not work in connection with a national transportation system which is supposed to serve the whole country.
The railroads were getting a subsidy of $108 million a year back in 1967, and the legislation passed in that year was designed to reduce the amount of that subsidy by about $14 million, so that inside of eight years no subsidy whatever would be forthcoming. This reduction would be accomplished by allowing the railways to charge whatever rates they wished. Well, we have seen the reduction of subsidies in one form and the building up of subsidies in another. It is time Canadians realised that we have to do much better than we have done so far in managing the railroads. We have to accept the fact that living in a
October 18, 1973

country four or five thousand miles in breadth, a country which needs to be tied together, the subsidy idea was not bad at all.
If we study the operations of some of the finest railroads in the world, we find they are subsidized. Even in Japan, with its heavy population, railroad operations have to be subsidized to a large extent. This is true of railways in the United States, too. I have already referred to Penn Central. I should like to read what Mr. Perlman, one of the brilliant railroaders of his day, had to say about the decline of that railroad.
I say that under the present system of regulation, under the present system of subsidies to the other three forms of transportation, under the system where we are not allowed to make rates competitive with other modes, it is a dying system. I still say the steel wheel on the steel rail is the most efficient form of transportation in the world. And it is being killed. We are not letting it die, it is being killed. I think it is a tragedy today to see it being killed that way. All I say, as a taxpayer, is: Treat them all alike. Don't give any of them subsidies-or subsidize them all.
Those views are still current in the minds of many people. Recently the government held a western economic conference and one of the subjects discussed was the transportation problem we encounter in the west. The act of 1967 has proved a colossal failure. It might have worked all right in other parts of Canada, but in the west it has been a colossal failure. The government has not even attempted to wrestle with this issue. Railway finance bills are brought before parliament. None of them are getting passed. No logical answers are given to explain how the railways are financing their operations without them. The government is reluctant to amend the transportation legislation of 1967 in any way. At the same time, the indebtedness of Air Canada has grown and parliament has yet to conduct a searching examination of the direction in which the corporation's affairs are going.
In 1967, the interest on Air Canada's debt amounted to $13.9 million. Today, it is $20 million. It is time we took stock of the direction in which we are moving, both in railroading and in air transportation. I spoke earlier about the long-term debt of Canadian National which has grown to around $1,894 million. In 1951, it was down to $615 million. Then, with the heavy expenditure during the years of dieselization in the 'fifties it rose by $630 million. Today, as I noted, it is $1,894 million, another $600 million between the 'sixties and now.
I see the purpose of this legislation is to provide funds for the building of more railway track and the purchasing of more equipment at a cost of $167.5 million. As late as last year, we were concerned in the Transport Committee about the accident rate of the CN and I was surprised to learn that only 19 per cent of the rolling stock of that company has Timken bearings in it. There is still 81 per cent of the CN rolling stock-or it might be this figure relates to all railroads-which has the old hot box problem, and most accidents are caused by this defect. Where has the company been spending the money? We do not seem to be getting value for it when, on examining the expenditure made by the CNR on equipment, we find we are still with the old hot box problem.
We see the CN developing turbo trains. Every now and then they make an experimental run from Montreal to Toronto to determine whether or not any improvements
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada have been made. No one appears to have questioned this expenditure and considered whether this form of turbo train is feasible. The Japanese are experimenting with the magnetic train. The power of magnets is used to run these cars; there are no wheels on the trains at all. I note that the CN is taking a look at the possibility of running such trains at speeds up to 300 miles an hour between Toronto and Montreal using the magnetic track principle. If this turns out to be feasible, surely we do not need two airports in Montreal and two in Toronto. But no one has really examined the proposal yet.
Recently some new bilateral air agreements have been completed with the United States, and it is of interest to note that the U.S. got the first jump at servicing Canadian cities. The odd thing about these agreements is that because of shortage of fuel in the U.S. they may not be able to take advantage of this part of the agreements. Certainly we should have had the opportunity of servicing American cities to the extent the United States has of servicing Canadian cities. I think the whole series of agreements was a mistake and should be re-examined as soon as possible.
At times I wonder how Ait Canada operates. A few years ago it introduced what was called a regional air policy, which I thought was a good concept. But the surprising thing about it has been the growth of regional air lines. We gaves these regional air carriers all the short, non-profitable runs with perhaps one or two good ones thrown in, yet they made a real success out of these short and mostly poor runs.
Why, then, is Air Canada still piling up its present debt structure? Pacific Western, an airline operating between Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver and places in northern Canada, has developed into the third largest airline in Canada. It is almost of national status. That airline operated an airbus service between Edmonton and Calgary that was so successful that Air Canada quit running between those two cities completely; they just could not compete with the managerial expertise of private enterprise.
I am suffering under the illusion that if we allowed private initiative to develop a similar airbus service between Montreal and Toronto, it would immediately prove to be a successful arrangement and Air Canada would have difficulty competing. A few years ago Air Canada declared it would commence an airbus service between Montreal and Toronto, but it has never come about. At least, any time I have tried to get on it I have been unable to do so.
The old story that has been running around here for years is that we should sell Air Canada. It was never explained whether or not Air Canada was to be taken over by the Canada Development Corporation. Is the financial structure of Air Canada to be separated from that of the CNR? That question has not been answered either. If Air Canada continues to relinquish some of its routes within Canada to some of the regional airlines, I would not be a bit surprised if the growth of the airline industry of this country proved to be second to none in the world. I say this because we are fortunate in having fuel for our
26635-14}

October 18, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada planes. The United States might have to shut down a lot of its big jet routes this winter owing to shortage of fuel.
Another matter that has always bothered me is this. Generally speaking, when aircraft become too small for the national airline they are sold to one of the regional air carriers. Why was not the Viscount sold far earlier to some of the regional air carriers? Air Canada kept the Viscounts flying until they could hardly fly any longer. The regional air carriers never bought them. As soon as they came up for sale, the regional carriers said that although it was a sturdy aeroplane to fly, it was the most expensive aircraft to keep in the air anywhere in the world and therefore they would not touch it. They said it was uneconomic and they would go broke trying to run it. Yet Air Canada kept them for 22 or 23 years; they were their real workhorses. Was this contented socialism at work, or is it a bad example of a contented management that was not prepared to scrap an aircraft and to use initiative? I really question the motivation of the management of that airline in regard to that particular decision.
Then instead of getting rid of the Viscounts earlier than they did, Air Canada bought a bigger Viscount, the Vanguard. They could not sell the Vanguards at all on the North American continent; they had to give them away, almost, to a country in Africa. The aircraft just could not compete economically. It was not a bad plane to fly in, but it just could not compete economically with other aircraft that were for sale. So the Vanguards had a very short life. They should never have been purchased in the first place; that was a colossal error. Here again, was this the action of a contented executive that was not prepared to look around or try a little harder?
These are some of the questions that arise when we examine air policy. Perhaps the regional air carriers should have a little larger share. According to an article not long ago in the Montreal Gazette, Mr. Pratte said, "We can do better", meaning that Air Canada can do better. I am glad he thinks so, because it is obvious to a lot of people that they should be doing better.
Then the government built the No. 2 air terminal at Toronto, and every member of the House of Commons has had a kick at this one. Most people consider it an inefficient terminal, difficult to manage and expensive to run. Again, was this government interference in the management of an airline which is government-owned but which should be run independently of government?
I think it is high time the officials of Air Canada and the CNR appeared before the transport committee of this House so the committee can examine their operations very carefully. Just recently Mr. Baldwin, one of the chief managers of Air Canada, took an early retirement. Was this the result of disagreement or disharmony within the executive of Air Canada? To me, his action was suspicious and requires examination.
There is one other point I want to make before closing. I return to the concept of socialism with which I started. It is high time we examined this concept, and for two reasons. We know that the present government is able to do things with the help of its partners on this side of the House. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet are able to do more with the present marriage in the House of Commons so far as socialism is concerned than they

could prior to the marriage. The socialist transportation experts of the NDP say that the trouble with the CNR is its national debt. The national debt of the CNR is 2.2 per cent of its gross operating income.
I ask my friends to our left whether they would advocate that any corporation cannot give up 3 per cent of its gross income and not go broke, but can continue to operate with a profit. They are always talking about the large corporations making a big rip-off, but 3 or 4 per cent is peanuts to them. That does not bother a big corporation at all. Yet the members of the NDP try to say that the long outstanding debt of the CNR is the cause of the CNR's poor financial showing. It amounts to only 2.2 per cent. The CPR's interest on debt is greater than that. Those members must examine the whole problem a little further.
The CNR is very labour-intensive; labour plays a very prominent role. In his book "Canadian National Railroad History," G. R. Stevens suggests that almost $2 out of every $3 that the railroad earns is spent on labour. That gives us some idea of the prominent position that labour plays in the success story of the CNR.
During my remarks a while ago hon. members to my left were worried when I referred to Penn Central problems in the United States. They said the railroads in the United States do not have a public conscience. That party and the main support of that party, the unions, must also display a public conscience if they seriously want the CNR to come up with a better financial picture. Having said that, I will allow someone else to continue this debate. Before the debate closes or the bill is allowed to pass, surely we should have an explanation as to how CNR and Air Canada have been financed without a bill such as this, for three years.

speechtext:
We do not know how they are being financed. We do not know why there was never an audit of the CNR financial statement. Because there was no audit, the annual report could not be referred to the committee for discussion. I said that I agree with a number of questions asked by the hon. member for Crowfoot, but I have a lot of difficulty with his conclusions. He spent a good deal of his time making what I felt to be a snide attack on the concept of socialism and socialistic thinking. He was very gentle about it, in contrast with his usual stand; he was most gentle about it tonight.
To back up his argument he used some quotations, out of context, from Mr. Gaibraith's magnificent book entitled "The New Industrial State". I read that book past page 2. What Mr. Galbraith was principally concerned about was the fact that the multicorporation, the private enterprise business corporation, was stronger than national governments. It was not that socialism had the upper hand, but the multicoporation, operating with massive capital in various countries, was going to be a threat to the national or sovereign governments of those countries. He was concerned about the fact that private enterprise, which has no democratic roots, was going to be stronger than freely elected governments.
The hon. member said-this amused me-that individuals, industries, concerns and enterprises paid out of the public purse lacked incentive and because of that were not efficient. He cited a number of examples which he used to explain why Air Canada and CNR might have had some problems. If that argument is going to be applied to those industries or crown corporations paid out of the public purse, it might as well be applied to the hon. member for Crowfoot. Outside of his cowboy business he is paid out of the public purse-and no one would want to suggest that the hon. member for Crowfoot lacks incentive.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Crowfoot knows I would never question his diligence, his competence, his conscientiousness or anything else publicly.
As a result of the meeting with a number of men who have had up to 30 years experience with the railway, I think I can say with a good deal of sincerity that they want the railway to run successfully. I was a little disappointed to hear the hon. member for Crowfoot, at the conclusion of his address, suggest that the men also had a responsibility to see that the railway is successful, almost implying that somehow because of their lack of co-operation they were responsible for the problems associated with the railways. I think the situation is quite the reverse. I believe it is the errors of management which have caused the difficulty, and now management wants the men to bail it out and subsidize transportation by means of the payment of lousy wages.
We tried to correct that situation through a special debate and found that when the vote came there was a difference between 34 cents and 38 cents. We know how the Conservative Party voted. However, that was better by four cents than the Liberal Party proposed. I do not have any figures, because it is almost impossible to obtain a statement from Canadian National in terms of a cost accounting, certainly on a regional basis, but it has been suggested that because of problems in respect of transportation in the Vancouver area the CNR in that region has lost $3 million.
The Canadian Pacific Railway is working to overcapacity and Canadian National Railways are not able to deliver the goods. We are concerned about a shortage of boxcars for B.C. interior lumber and for prairie grain. Do you

know where those boxcars are? They are on the sidings, loaded. There is no room in the Vancouver yards and they are stored in many small, out of the way places because they cannot unload the cars in Vancouver.
Management is blaming the rail strike for the delay. The cause is not the rail strike at all. The cause is the wages paid to the truckers which are so low, about $1 an hour below the prevailing rate, that fully one-third of the truckers who would unload the cars have resigned in the last four months. This is why they cannot unload those cars. The truckers went to work for private industry and private truck lines under a Teamsters Union contract which rewards them a good deal higher.
Where are the 200 cars we need so desperately in the interior of British Columbia? My answer is that they are sitting on the sidings, loaded. That may not be of any concern. In the last few months 90 switchmen or yardmen, experienced men who can achieve the productivity which we need, have resigned because of poor morale. I have a list of these experienced people and the number of years they have been on the job. If I had time I could read out their names and when they joined the company.
When you lose such people, how can there be high productivity? How can the company retain these experienced people if the working conditions and pension benefits are so poor? I will deal with that matter in a little while. I have another list of employees, machinists in the Vancouver port yard, 20 per cent of whom have quit their jobs in the last few months. They include machine apprentices. Also, 18 per cent of the electricians in the Vancouver port yard have quit. There are 40 carmen of whom 10 have quit, or 25 per cent, after a minimum of four years and a maximum of 15 years experience.
I asked today whether the standing committee on transport could go out to look at this one problem. Of course, there are many other problems. All you have to do is ask the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). We have had the Harbours Board problem and many other problems. We also have many benefits. Just living there is a benefit. But we must not forget the problems.
Four months ago I put forward a motion in the standing committee on transport that we appoint a travelling committee to go out to hear these concerns and complaints. We are still considering it. The minister did give us some hope. He said he will contact the CNR management and ask them for an explanation. I know what kind of an explanation he will get. No more than a week ago the CN management told the union representatives that nobody was quitting and that they really did not have any problems. Yet I have a list of the men who have quit. At least 100 of the approximately 400 men in the Vancouver yard have left the work force.
We have no money for the men, but we can pay the hotel expenses of management personnel, those snoops, those promoters and master mechanics, who come out of Edmonton, Regina, Moose Jaw and other places to supervise and spy on the men. Do you know what they are doing? They are working to rule. The rules are the uniform code of operating rules. If the men break those rules, they get demerits; but if the company breaks those rules they get profit, because the company is its own policeman. There is
October 18, 1973

constant pressure and harassment of the men to break the rules to improve productivity. There are officials following the men around. They are just waiting for Chief Justice Emmett Hall's report and the Deutsch report, and I predict that if the reports are not favourable we will lose a lot more of them.
How can you increase productivity, have the boxcars unloaded, and provide boxcars in a boxcar-short country if there is that kind of low morale and lack of experienced people working in the yards? The philosophy outlined by the hon. member for Crowfoot is all very well, but these are practical problems that are bothering these people every day. They are resentful, bitter, and they are right; no one will get around that one. They also have other problems. They are in a minority in Canada. The railroad workers in British Columbia are in a minority among railroad workers in Canada. It is impossible for them to have any say in such unions as the IWA, the United Auto Workers, and perhaps the steel unions as well. It is impossible for them to gain their own autonomy, to gain control of their own union in Canada.
There are impediments in making any move under IRDI to get any kind of reasonable and meaningful Canadian autonomy in their union or even to influence their western chairman or national officers. They have to win a 25 per cent referendum among all the UTU workers or, in general, all the workers in both Canada and the United States, and they cannot even get the list of membership from the grand lodge. So what have they done? They have stopped paying their dues. They said to themselves that the only way in which they could get these people to listen to them was to hit them where it really hurts, which is in their pocketbooks. When they stopped paying their dues, CNR became worried because they have had a happy relationship with some of these rail unions. So the management said, "All right; if you do not pay your dues you do not get your seniority rights." So they will have to go back to paying their dues or they will lose the better jobs.
That is not all. The international office in Cleveland, Ohio-the international president, in fact-decided that some of these dues payers, or non-dues payers, are all in one locality and they should be disciplined. So they wrote the members of the CN local 1747 and the treasurer of CP local 442 and said that from then on all CN yardmen and yardmasters would be transferred to CP local 422. As if that was not enough, they said that none of the present officers on CN local 1747 would be permitted to seek office in the expanded CN-CP local 442 unless specifically approved by the Cleveland office. The officer who is in charge of CN local 1747 has never held back on his dues, yet because those two locals have been merged in a highhanded, bureaucratic and foreign manner he cannot even seek office.
I have outlined the litany of complaints against management. Here is their problem with their own union. So we see that they have a lot of trouble and no chance of winning any kind of change within 18 months because they are prevented from doing so by national legislation. Therefore they are fed up. That is why they are leaving, and that is why there is loss of productivity on the railroads. That is why they are embittered. They have agreed
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada to work to rule and to withdraw their dues because they have no other way of fighting.
In addition, they have had an increase of only 34 cents in the last package, and we directed them back to work as if they were slave labour. The best estimate is that the men are subsidizing the CN by about $500 million a year in underpaid wages. In addition to that, CN has $900 million of the men's pension money. The board of directors has invested this matter. I do not think there are any CN men on the board of directors of the CN pension plan. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will certainly correct me if I am wrong on this, because he is our expert on pensions as well as on many other things. That money is invested at 8 per cent to 14 per cent interest by the CN pension board. But anything over a 3 per cent return to that fund reduces CNR's obligation. That is criminal and fraudulent. It is the men's money, $900 million, yet they have a niggardly pension.
.
The other day the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pleaded with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to abase himself before the CNR pension directors so that the retired men can get a little bit more. All he got was a lecture about the work being done by Mr. John Deutsch. That indicates lack of understanding of the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
People get extremely angry about this subject. The union officers in the western region can sign on behalf of the men for anything, and their contracts can be legal without any ratification of the members. That is not good enough. How on earth can you ever have any kind of morale, spirit, joie de vie or anything like that in such a situation? The whole thing stinks, and it is time we did something about it. That is why I am trying to do something about it now. I want to apply some pressure, if ever this little diatribe of mine gets out of this building, on the CNR management in Vancouver. Incidentally, I hear that a committee of parliamentarians is going out to Vancouver this weekend. Perhaps there is something that 60 or 80-member committee could do.
Much more could be said about the CNR. I do not know how long I have been speaking, perhaps for half an hour-

speechtext:
The hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) is always pleased if I get up to throw a rounder at the unions. I don't blame him. I do not think they have the answers to everything. No one has. But there are things here that, as Canadian nationalists, we should be doing something about, and there are things we should be doing to satisfy these people's grievances.
For a few moments I would like to speak about the Air Canada situation, following the general line of the hon. member for Crowfoot. I am not going to discuss the technicalities of the archaic Viscounts and Vanguards. With respect to the reluctance, I suggest that maybe the management was a bit gun-shy when it came to a decision on spending money because it felt some parliamentarian would get up and say the public corporation was wasteful, or maybe management was just being thrifty; it may have

October 18, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
been a bad decision by management. Mr. Speaker, if there were no bad management decisions, why would we need bankruptcy legislation? We need it to assist private corporations to bail themselves out when they make bad decisions. No company, private or public, has a monopoly on bad decisions or on good ones. Nevertheless, there is concern about Air Canada among some of the people I represent on the west coast.
In this connection I would like to read from a letter received from an Air Canada pilot. Naturally for reasons best known to myself, I would prefer to make him anonymous. I might say that I have had conversations with others who are a little concerned about the situation, especially people who live in the west. Here I am speaking not only of pilots but of the general cabin staff. This pilot is concerned that the "gravy runs" are not going to Air Canada. That is one of the reasons Air Canada's profit picture is' not as bright as it might be. He suggests that when it comes to passing out new routes, whether to Milan or China, Air Canada is usually last in line. In fact, it could be argued that regional air carriers are getting good routes and are skimming off the profit. I am not making that statement in this context but I know it has happened in other fields. I know that the cable companies serving our cities get their profit by skimming the populous regions and not giving service where the population is scarce.
This pilot also says that aside from Air Canada being last in line when it comes to handing out the juicy routes, it is "a very eastern-oriented airline, as demonstrated in the latest aircraft and pilot assignment list." He enclosed that list. Obviously, 1974 is going to be a big expansion year for airlines. According to this list, 28 crews are to be added to Toronto and 28 or 29 crews to Montreal, bases which are just 400 or 500 miles apart. But in terms of expansion there is not one extra crew member going to Vancouver for the 1974 season.
Pilots with three or four years training can operate out of central Canada, if they care to live there; but people with that kind of experience can never become much above a first officer in western Canada. This is basically inequitable and unfair. I think the Toronto and Montreal bases tend to be favoured. Whether this is because representatives from those areas have more political clout than westerners, I do not know; but we do know there are 23 representatives from the city of Toronto and 27 from Montreal and we cannot match their voices in western Canada.
The pilot I have referred to writes:
While countries like New Zealand and Australia ponder the right of CP Air flying into their countries, possibly Air Canada should have the door of the Orient open to them via the Vancouver airport. This leads us to wonder how and why the China run was ever awarded to CP in the first place. Using the reasoning that they already fly to the east is not valid. It might apply to a shipping company, but not an airline flying 550-mile an hour jets.
This and a number of things I have said this evening will indicate why we are not very pleased about seeing this Air Canada financing bill only from time to time. It is like the magicians' card trick-now you see it, now you don't. It is used as a sandwich-filler. If there is nothing more to talk about, let the boys whack away at it. I am sure the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen)

must say to himself, "Let the boys hammer away and get it out of their systems, as long as we do not have a debate that is too concentrated."
The government does not really care whether we deal with this bill or not. But in the meantime the CNR is losing 18 per cent of its work force, some 7,000 men, each year. As a result of recent attrition, 23 per cent of the CN work force have been on the job less than two years. There is no way in which we can increase productivity of this national railway and provide Canada with the services it needs if we have an inexperienced work force. Here we have a work force that is inadequately equipped, that is bitter and has low morale.
The new training scheme for engineers is an example of the frustration which is experienced. For the past three years I have been trying to get an answer from the regulatory body known as the CTC on the question of who is in charge of a train when a student is abroad with the engineer, along with a master mechanic. We cannot get that answer from the CTC. Mr. Speaker, you may recall that every winter we lose railroaders in the Fraser Canyon because of snowfalls. There is an example now of a man being charged because he refused to hand over the running of his train. He was the engineer, and the master mechanic ordered him to hand over to a student. He refused because it is not clear who would have been responsible had the train been involved in an accident while the student was at the controls. You would think that would be an easy thing to straighten out. Just call the CTC and get an answer: find out who is in charge of the train, the engineer or the master mechanic. But we cannot get an answer, Mr. Speaker, so these frustrations pile one upon the other. These molehills build up into mountains of dissatisfaction and are bound to have an effect upon the railroad.
If we put the two systems together we might find that we have a rationalized transportation system, half private and half public, and it might work to the advantage of the Canadian public. It is certainly not working to anybody's satisfaction, today.

It is no coincidence that we have the CN financing bill before us tonight at the same time as the fifth game of the world series. It seems to me that nobody wants to interfere with the world series, so it is a case of let's bring on the CN financing bill and maybe make a few frivolous remarks and pass a few jokes, then get on with more serious business tomorrow. Indeed, it seems that some members treat the occasion of the CN financing bill as an annual joke. When we speak we know that not much is going to come out of it. At least, that is the feeling I get this evening. Even the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has not thought it necessary to be here.
A couple of evenings ago I was in the company of some friends from western Canada and one was asking, "Where is my wandering bull tonight?" I am wondering where the Minister of Transport is tonight.

speechtext:
He should be here taking part in the CN financing bill. I wonder if the government is trying to switch the ministers around again. They got into all kinds of trouble when they had the Minister of Transport and the minister of DREE occupying their previous roles, so they were switched. I do not know what is happening now, but transportation is becoming a colossal joke in the House of Commons day after day. We see evidence of this every day with the Minister of Transport.
A few weeks ago when the strike was on I saw a clip on one of the national television programs. I believe Norman DePoe was doing the voice-over. It was bits of an old film about the original railroading days. It gave me a feeling of nostalgia and identification with the railwaymen, and a remembrance of the old cowboy movies and the part the railwaymen played in them. Do hon. members remember the sounds and the music of that era? Even today you can turn on the radio and hear Johnny Cash or the blues singers with their beautiful railway songs about the times when people were building something. People across the nation were opening up our frontiers, allowing the country to grow and develop.
Today one TV commercial talks about building "the Canadian dream". Mr. Speaker, if you say that and were from some other country, you might believe it. You might believe they are building the great Canadian dream, seeing the prosperity and involvement across the nation, with CP and CN building that dream. I would like some of the people who get hundreds of thousands of dollars for such advertising to go to some parts of Canada that have made the headlines, and see the extent of this great Canadian dream. I think we are going to get a revival of the blues for a different reason-people are going to mourn the passing of the great transportation days. The blues singers are now singing the blues about what is happening today. When we talk about transportation, we talk about the future of our country, Mr. Speaker. I doubt if an industrial nation has ever grown to greatness without a transportation system that was modern in that day and age.
At a meeting of the Atlantic Advisory Council last week the chairman said something to the effect that the transportation system in the Atlantic provinces in no way impedes the economic growth of that area. I can speak with some knowledge of the Atlantic area, Mr. Speaker, and I say we cannot reach any great level of economic growth unless we take issue with the present transportation system.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
I have listened to members from the Prairies and British Columbia speak, and it seems to be the consensus that we are wasting our time with all our talk about economic policies and DREE programs unless we are willing to provide the country with a modern transportation system. I believe it was in 1885 that the last spike was driven in the national railway. Mr. Speaker, almost a century ago we had a national transportation system, a brand new system. It had taken the imagination of our greatest leaders of various political stripes decades
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada to put it into effect in face of the financial difficulties, scandals and political upheaval that surrounded it.
Imagine the railwaymen of that day. The railwayman's cap is to me a symbol of the workingman and the growth of industrial development. These people put together a system that must have been a hundred years ahead of what we have today, in terms of the comparative economic needs of the country. We hear talk of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, their industrial incentive programs and loans programs, but we hear nothing about transportation except that a province is willing to negotiate an extra bit of blacktop somewhere on a road in an Atlantic province. Our transportation system is archaic compared to conditions of a decade ago. If I may be forgiven for being a little parochial, I will tell hon. members something of our own transportation today compared to ten years ago or longer. I would like to get this on the record and in some small way try to tell the Canadian people of a problem we have. I do not think it is unique, but it is an indication of the seriousness of our transportation problem.
In 1949 we became part of Canada. Under term 32 of the Terms of Union we concluded an agreement with the federal government which was signed by our Fathers of Confederation who certainly could not look forward many generations. Nor can anybody look ahead, today, to the future with any great certainty. But in that day and age they realized transportation should remain some kind of government responsibility and they placed in the act, under term 32, a provision that Canada should provide a link between mainland Canada and the island part, the province of Newfoundland, and arrange for the existence of a transportation system carrying goods and services commensurate with the needs of the province.
This was spelling out in the Terms of Union between Newfoundland and Canada, the marriage contract, if you want to call it that, in 1949. In that day and age we did not depend very much on a modern transportation system. We were more involved in coastal trade because we had literally hundreds of our own freighters, schooners and other *ships which used to provide us with goods from Europe, the Caribbean, the New England states and even from that foreign country which was called Canada. But we did have a fairly adequate transportation system. As a result of our entry into confederation we got a "Go" ferry operation which provided a link over 100 miles of water from North Sydney to Port aux Basques. Today, in 1973, we are almost totally dependent on outside sources for all the goods which are needed to serve 500,000 Canadians on the east coast of this country. I should like mainland Canadians to recognize this.
If we were arguing in support of a transportation system to ship goods in from Japan or some other foreign country, I would expect some Canadians to get their backs up. But today we are almost totally dependent as a province on goods shipped from central Canada. We are the most captive of all the parts of Canada in terms of consumer demand. We are virtually non self-supporting in all areas of consumer goods. We are an exporting province. We export a variety of raw resources. We export a large amount of mineral resources, mainly from Labrador and

October 18, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada some from the island part of the province, and a tremendous quantity of fish products which go mainly to places in the United States. We are beginning to export a variety of wood products, paper from both the east and west coasts, and linerboard which, by the way, is going to Montreal now and serving the needs of some of the strike-ridden parts of Quebec.
We are an exporter of raw resources to other parts of Canada and North America. We are an importer of every type of consumer goods. We get up in the morning, and all the dishes we have come from Ontario; the knives and forks come from Ontario. The stoves we use come from somewhere in Ontario or Quebec, or some other part of this industrial nation of ours. We go to bed in the evening, and all our bedclothes, the bed, television set and furniture come from central Canada. Everything we have in our provinces is imported. We are a captive market, and our imports from mainland Canada over the last ten years have about doubled. I calculated a few weeks ago that we have in the last 12 months increased our imports from central Canada by about 15 per cent.
We have a transportation system today which is grossly inferior to what we had in 1969. First of all, in 1969 we had a passenger service which ran across the whole of the 580 miles of the island. At that time the minister of transport was Jack Pickersgill who used to be the member for the riding I now represent. He afterward became the czar of transport as chairman of the transportation commission. I have admiration for him as a parliamentarian, but I lost a great deal of respect for him as a result of transportation decisions which he made.
The CNR, under the calculated guidance of the minister, cooked the books in such a manner as to enable Canadian National to argue that the rail transport service was a non-paying venture-as if it was a paying venture anywhere in Canada. The end result was that they abandoned the rail passenger service and gave us a bus system. Every time I talk about the bus system I am reminded of an old colleague of mine with whom I had a bite to eat about a week ago, the former member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, Mr. Ambrose Peddle, who sat in this House and made a tremendous plea. I would call him the father of the effort to get back a rail system when he spoke out in almost his first speech against the decision of Canadian National to abandon this service. We did everything in our power, next to short-circuiting the whole activity of parliament, to get that system back. But we lost.
The CN had decided, with all the inside track it had with the Canadian Transport Commission, that the service was going, and it went. I can remember rolling a barrel full of signatures collected from 31,000 Newfoundland people-the biggest petition ever taken up in Canada-protesting the abandonment of the rail passenger service. The petition could not be presented to the House because the rules provide that petitions must be presented in such a magnificent fashion, under such formal conditions, that it is not feasible to do so. So what we did was to present a token petition to symbolize the 31,000 petitioners who protested the abandonment of the service. And we still lost, because CN decided that we were not going to get any rail passenger service in the future.

I have perhaps put my finger on one of the most significant aspects of the matter we are discussing today. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that we in this chamber have any control over the transportation system in this country? Do you think that even the Minister of Transport is able to exercise any control? So we get ourselves a big department of government. Most of us haven't enough ability to run the average office. I find myself struggling from day to day to keep two people functioning efficiently, let alone manage a department of government. Yet a minister takes office; and if he is in office for 25 years he might know about railway operations as much as an experienced railway worker, let alone the manager of the corporation. Consequently, this being only one of a minister's responsibilities, he is bamboozled into believing whatever he happens to be fed.
I found myself during the last few days trying to get some kind of responsible reaction from the Minister of Transport. But he is so defensive of CN you would think his grandfather owned it. He stands up in the House of Commons and loses his temper. Have you seen him? We had a little Pekingese one time. He would bite your legs off if you looked at him the wrong way. That is what the Minister of Transport reminds me of. When you ask him about the CN you would think you were asking about his closest relative. This is as a result of what they are feeding him. I remember last Thursday. By the way, I have been the best dispatcher the CNR has had for some time. In the last six or seven weeks I have been involved in trying to route a carload of goods out of North Sydney over to Newfoundland. I think there would have been almost an economic standstill on the northeast coast of our province if I had not become a CN dispatcher. The only thing is, I didn't get paid for it.
Last week a businessman phoned me and said, "We have a hotel ready to move into. Our move has been delayed for over a month. Is there any way you can put a spark under the rear ends of CN people to move a carload of freight for us?" I phoned and I said, "Boys, can you move this carload?" And they moved it. They phoned the minister immediately and he said, "Look, if he ever throws anything at you, just tell him that the only thing he has ever had moved, or the thing that he classifies as an emergency, is a load of furniture." This is what is surprising to me- that the communication I had with the North Sydney agent got up to the Minister of Transport to the point at which he was to be armed with his defences-"You moved a carload of furniture". He also had the statistics on the number of backlogged cars in North Sydney a year ago.
This is the way they have armed him, and instead of saying to those fellows, "Look, you bunch of beggars and you deceitful fellows who are trying to sell me this line of goods, we want something done about it," he stands up and tries to protect the Canadian National Railways. I would like to see people in other countries like Japan, which has one of the most modern transportation systems in the world, especially the monorail system, and even England, which has a railway system which would put us to shame, come in and analyse what we have got going in this country of ours. I think that even Newfie jokes would have nothing on that. These people would laugh at us for weeks; indeed, it might almost stop the war.
October 18, 1973

We are not able to handle goods and services adequately with the present transportation system in the Atlantic provinces. We are not able to develop economically as we would like. Yet in this part of Canada there is one of the highest unemployment rates in the western world, and this has been so since day one, 1867. You would think that one government at least would have the imagination and vision to recognize that lack of economic growth is the reason for our high unemployment rate. This is why the government should harness a program that would not only give us the transportation facilities we need but would in the process help us overcome our unemployment difficulties within five or ten years.
I just want to set the record straight on a few things, Mr. Speaker. I am disappointed that the Minister of Transport has not had the decency tonight to be here and take part in this debate, placing on record the argument for CN. He is the spokesman in this House for CN and his absence is a disappointment to every member of the House. Ten years ago CNR guaranteed three-day delivery of express goods from points in Toronto and Quebec to Newfoundland. I know this is a frivolous subject to the sophisticated members from the large centres of Canada. One of the problems in this House is that we have now become such a great nation that divergent parts of the country are almost like ruptured appendices: they should be cut out.
I have gone off at a tangent and I will get back to my point, but first let me say there does not seem to be any responsiveness on the part of the federal government to the different needs of the regions of this country. If there is a problem in a major area with a large population which would have a tremendous effect on the political fortunes of a particular party, then the attention paid to that problem is magnificent. But if the member from the Yukon raises a problem, or there is a problem in the riding of Skeena, in Prince Rupert, in the Athabasca area, in Timiskaming or in some other part of northern Ontario-it almost seems to be out of order these days to talk about northern Ontario-then the situation is entirely different. One almost hears a groan from the House these days when northern Ontario is mentioned. There are only four members from P.E.I.-and do they have a real voice in this House?
I have talked about problems till I am black and blue in the face. I am getting completely frustrated and so are the people I represent. I see the Minister of Transport making a momentary appearance for 60 seconds. He will be back again in a moment because I see he has his notes all ready, prepared for him by Mr. MacMillan of Montreal, no doubt.
I am concerned that the problems of my region are not being properly received or transmitted. I am sure that in the last five years the seven members from the province I represent have had their say in this House; I am convinced of that. I am convinced they have told their stories about our problems. But I am equally convinced that there has not been much reception of those problems. Unless there is a better way in this federal system for the government to recognize the legitimacy of what we say, then I do not feel like tearing around the countryside in my eagerness to be a Canadian.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
Recently a little strike took place. As a Canadian, I was embarrassed to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) get up in the House and try to say the reason for the strike was that the workers would not move our goods. Even Newfoundlanders can go on strike, he said. No one bothered to tell him that at no time was there any agreement during the strike to move goods across 100 miles of water. Unfortunately there was an agreement with regard to passenger service, but because of some upheavel that agreement was broken and as a result personal hardship was caused. But there was no agreement to move freight. Along with the Premier of P.E.I. we argued constantly that the federal government had an over-riding responsibility, under the constitution, to see that goods were able to move between the provinces of Canada. As a result of a three-week strike there will be a backlog of freight until the spring of 1974.
I know it is a waste of time talking about this. I am not saying it is the media's fault, but I am sick and tired of going outside this House and finding a cubbyhole to talk into the tape machines they have about this problem. For one reason or another the government will not recognize that we do have a second-class system, one that is worse than the system we had 50 years ago. Then today the minister had the absolute gall to say that if there is an emergency he will make some special effort. He does not recognize the fact that goods have been tied up in our transportation system since September 3, six weeks ago, which in itself is an emergency.
I can tell hundreds of stories concerning the impact that the transportation system of this country has had on the economy of our coast in the last number of years. It got to the point last year where one small businessman who had been receiving fresh goods shipped in from Toronto found they were arriving so late so frequently that the shipper decided not to ship to Newfoundland any more. The only compensation he was offered was that CN or Air Canada agreed to pay if the goods were spoiled. But we have to wait so long for our money that these goods are now shipped south of the border where the market is just as good.
Ten years ago, in 1962 or 1963, we were guaranteed three-day delivery of goods sent express to Newfoundland from central Canada. Today the minimum time express goods from central Canada take to get to Newfoundland is ten days. I have been told by people on the firing-line, people right in the sheds who receive the freight, that they are lucky to get it under two weeks; usually it takes much longer than that. That is the quality of the service we get.
I am disappointed that "his nibs" was not in the House earlier to hear some of the complaints that we have brought to his attention as the eminent Minister of Transport. We are not standing up in this House because we like to hear ourselves talk; we have legitimate complaints to make about the quality of CN service. Instead of attacking members of parliament who say they have a problem, why does not the Minister of Transport call some of the fellows in charge of this great national system into his office and start asking them some questions?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
