speechtext:
It sounds like playing games.

October 18, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
They are playing a political game. If we had not kicked up the fuss we did, we would have 1,500 cars in North Sydney today. Can you imagine CN officials saying to the Minister of Transport that they want a special effort made because they are not moving the freight fast enough? September 19 was the day the minister told us to learn to swim, and since then I have been taking swimming lessons every day. He said the backlog would be moved in two weeks. That was on September 19. Today is October 18, one month later. There are exactly the same number of cars today in North Sydney. Cars are sitting in the Moncton system.
Hon. members may be interested in knowing what happens to goods leaving Toronto or Montreal destined for the Atlantic region. The Atlantic region is able to accommodate only so many cars. The first delay is in Montreal. The cars then go to Moncton, where they are again delayed. That is the second stage of delivery. I have been told by businessmen that cars have been sitting in Moncton since September 3. They eventually move to Truro and then to North Sydney. Halifax is another terminal point. After that, someone eventually recognizes the problem and they get to Port aux Basques, a western terminal, then on to the southern centres of distribution.
No matter what is done with the existing boats and existing facilities, there is practically no way of improving the transportation system into our province. That is a fact. The only thing that could be done in the short haul, and this could not last very long, would be to keep it at the level it is now, with a backlog of 500 or 600 cars. If 10 or 12 Hercules aircraft were put into operation for a couple of weeks, we might be able to move the non-essentials. They are non-essential in the sense that people will not starve if they are not moved, but they are essential because people demand and need the service. Also, many things are important for our economic growth. This would clear up the problem in the short haul.
Some fairly major decisions will have to be made with regard to the province I represent. More ports will have to be opened. Some will have to be winter ports such as there are on the south coast, perhaps at Bay d'Espoir. Others will have to be built on the east coast. There is a harbour facility which was hardly completed when the government took out Clarke Steamships. Clarke Steamships was receiving a subsidy which was taken away three years ago. There are multimillion-dollar storage facilities there, with nothing moving through them because neither this minister nor anyone else is willing to go there and find out what is the problem unless people like myself take up the time of the House to bring it to the attention of the minister. Tomorrow there will be 15 people from CNR feeding the minister junk and garbage about the quality of service they are providing. Sometimes I do not blame him for accepting that. As I have said before, he is one man, with a big department.
If the minister would recognize the urgency of what we are saying, I would be very happy. Some major changes have to be made if our province is going to survive as an economic entity in Canada. For the past five years CN have let the whole thing slide. It has become one big mess. No one bothers about it too much unless there is a real

logjam like there is at the present time. That is why we are in this House every day, crying about the problem. We will be here every day until someone does something about it. I cannot wait to get my teeth into some of those CNR fellows when they appear before our committee to explain the mess on the east coast today.
I am very serious when I say that our people are becoming extremely frustrated. The situation is becoming almost contradictory. We should be, and have been, the most exuberant Canadians in this nation. We have the spark and fire of Canadianism throughout our whole province. However, we are getting to the point where we feel ours is a voice in the wilderness. No one listens to us and, even more important, nobody gives a damn. I hope the minister will consider our economic problems and look into the serious backlog that will take until the spring of 1974 to clear up. If we were a powerful part of the country with 50 or 60 members, we could handle ourselves easily. We would defeat this government and get in somebody else. If they did not handle our problem, we would get rid of them as well.
We have the most problems and the least amount of power. Our problems are almost boring because they affect so few people. It is like someone talking about the Indian problem or problems in the Yukon. People are bored because it affects too few people. Because of psychological irritants, some patients end up going batty. It is these little things that are causing a tremendous amount of damage to the fabric of confederation.
My time is almost up. I want to say something which I have thought about for some time. What would happen to some central Canada industries if we were not a market for them? What would happen if we could negotiate our own trade deals with the European Economic Community and other parts of the world? What if we had our own currency and controlled our imports? I wonder how much would be lost to central Canada. I suppose no one has ever done the research to find out the impact that 500,000 people have on the market. What would happen if this market were lost to central Canada? What would happen in Oshawa? Cars stream into Newfoundland every day. What would it do to the employment situation in that part of Ontario? I do not know how much 500,000 people consume in food and material goods, but obviously this is a fairly important factor.
Every now and again we hear about equalization payments. Some members from Ontario get their backs up. It is as though we are the welfare part of the country. One fine day they will recognize the value of our great untapped resources, minerals and oil, to the economic security of North America. Perhaps then the mentality will change. In the interim, it might be wise for the government to have a bit of vision. We do not see this in governments today. Governments do not think a decade or two ahead. Most think about and react to yesterday's problems.
Has anyone ever given serious consideration to some form of subsidized freight rates in order that we may buy a car or other goods at the price they are being sold for in central Canada? Is this what Premier Lougheed talked about at the recent western economic conference? He talked about the need for major changes in transportation
October 18, 1973

costs to points divergent from central Canada. Not only do we buy our goods from Ontario, such as cars from Oshawa and washing machines from Toronto, but we have to pay substantially higher prices because of the freight costs involved. We are thankful that we can provide jobs, but we feel freight rates should be equalized so that goods cost the same in one part of the country as in another.
This is a big country, 5,000 miles wide and thousands of miles from north to south. Something should be done about our transportation system so that people in all parts of the country will feel they are part of Canada. At present, this is a real disadvantage. On the northeast coast of Canada, the north shore and possibly northern Ontario, people feel they have to pay a price for being part of confederation, without receiving the benefits.
I know I am wasting my breath in speaking to the minister along these lines. If he would even solve the problem of the backlog in North Sydney he would feel as good as Napoleon did after his escape from Elba. That would be an achievement for him. I do not expect him to become involved in the matter of monorails and cross-subsidies, because that would be an exceptional challenge. But he might keep this matter in the back of his mind, and some day when we stand and ask a question about the backlog, he might recognize it is legitimate and start talking to the big guns in Montreal who manage the great system of CN and are building this great dream for us in Canada.
Why does he not call them all in, put his finger in their mid-sections and say he is not satisfied? Why does he not look at the legislation to see whether he can pull a few strings in respect of these people? He must have some control. I get the impression that in talking about the railway we are talking about some little prince in the wilderness over whom no one has control. I should like to think that this spirited minister from Quebec, for whom I have great respect, would manifest some of that spirit when dealing with the great monopoly called Canadian National Railways and drag these people into his office and lay his cards on the table, so that some day he would be able to come here and tell us that these things will be done. I can tell him that if he did this we would have much more respect for him as the spokesman for Canadian National Railways.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-164 contains some recommendations regarding the state-owned corporations, the CNR and Air Canada, and when you study those recommendations you find that they are a bottomless pit able to swallow up any amount of money. We are given a forecast of possible expenditures between now and June or July 1974, but it is added that Parliament may be asked to vote additional moneys should those state-owned corporations be unable to finance themselves through their operating revenues. I would like to quote the following recommendations:
His Excellency the Governor General has recommended . . .
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada ... to extend the limit of refunding under the Canadian National Railway Refunding Act, 1955, to one billion dollars; to authorize Her Majesty to make loans to the Canadian National Railway Company and Air Canada to meet deficiencies in operating revenues to June, 1974 . . .
This means that should the amount now being requested, namely $669 million for the two State-owned corporations, be inadequate for their operations, we are empowered to vote additional amounts to meet the requirements. And I quote further:
. .. any such loans to be repaid from revenues of the Railway Company and Air Canada or, if revenues prove insufficient.. .
When the 669 million have been eaten up ...
... if revenues prove insufficient by subsequent deficit appropriation by Parliament.
This means that there are no limits. Therefore, if it is considered that there are no limits, then why give the figure of $669 million?
However, we are asking Parliament to standardize freight-rates throughout Canada so that western people do not have to pay more than the eastern Canadians for transportation from one area to another within Canada. If it costs a little more, what can the minister say for himself?-We have the power to vote supplementary credits! There is nothing to prevent us from doing it, but let us let justice prevail in all areas of the economy with respect to freight rates in Canada. That would solve the problem concerning the famous feed grains we wish to carry from west to east, that would solve the transportation problem from the east to central Canada as far as fish is concerned. Even if the minister said: We need $225,500,000 for extension and improvement purposes, etc. Out of that amount, $75,000 are allocated to new construction. I refer here to branch lines, etc. In clause 3 the government gives the estimated amounts for 1973 and I quote:
Road property	$138,978,000.10
Those 10 cents are important.
Branch lines Equipment Telecommunications Hotels
CN Tower Limited
13,000,000
31.897.000
25.946.000 5,679,000 8,800,000.15
As far as hotels are concerned, they have precious little to do with transport: Parliament is asked to vote $14 million to complete what is connected with hotels in Canada.
We are no longer dealing with the CNR or Air Canada but, after consideration of the government we must still compete with private entreprise and with the hotel trade in general. Thus, with respect to transport by the CNR or Air Canada, we are asked to vote such fabulous estimates to compete with private entreprise which is faced with increases in prices, taxes and cost of materials. Mr. Speaker, the bill now under consideration is an impediment to private entreprise. It is not honest competition.
Those who must buy trucks worth $40,000 or $50,000 to pull trailers have seen the price of their licence plates triple in the past seven or eight years; diesel oil now costs about twice as much as it did five years ago. The carriers must incur cost increases, while they have no other

Canadian National Railways and Air Canada income than the freight or transport rates they charge in their business. In addition, they must balance their budget and also pay fantastic amounts in income tax to the federal government which introduces a bill designed to compete instead of walking on one's feet, I wonder what it is, if not an unfair competition for private enterprise in the field of transportation.
As regards the services provided by these means of transportation, we have been asking for years that more suitable trains be put into operation between Ottawa and Montreal, Montreal and Quebec City, Montreal and Toronto, that the Trans-Canada, for instance, which runs between Halifax and Vancouver, be improved. Mr. Speaker, there is room for improvement and I feel that we should not be satisfied to provide hundreds of millions, even almost $1 billion a year at present, to enable them to pursue their unfair operations as regards private enterprise. This is where politics comes in, of course. Whether you call it the Canadian Transport Commission, with its control over the Department of Transport, those state-owned corporations have too many employees compared to private enterprise. Employment security is given as a pretext! Employment security paid by the Canadian people, no way! When there are too many employees in an area, they should be allowed to go and work somewhere else. It is simple as that. Mr. Speaker, one cannot always try to make his way through the economic conditions that prevail in crown corporations. Where there is one man employed in private enterprise, there are five in a crown corporation, in an attempt to secure votes for the next election. It has reached such a point that people must wear steel-tipped shoes so that their toes are not crushed when they tread upon one another's feet. We do not have anything against employment but this is an undertaking that is not economic, and the proof of this is that we are asked $100 millions every time to make up deficits. Moreover, they meddle in almost every field, including the hotel trade.
Mr. Speaker, the Creditists want better railway services across Canada. Let Parliament not only pass votes. For example, some say that useless expenditures are made. I will merely give you an example. Air Canada has three daily northbound flights: two Viscounts fly during the day and at night a DC-8 leaves Montreal flying directly to Val d'Or and then Rouyn. There, the aircraft empties and passengers embark for Montreal at 8:55 p.m. That is flight 553. It leaves Rouyn, stops again at Val d'Or and then flies to Montreal. When one knows that the take-off is the major cost element in a flight why does Air Canada not schedule a flight that would go directly to Val d'Or letting off passengers at that point and flying back to Montreal with new passengers. The Rouyn-Montreal flight would be shortened by at least three quarters of an hour and the corporation would save thousands of dollars.
Air Canada tells me that the Rouyn runway might not be long enough for a full plane. I talked to the Minister of Transport but he says that the runway is long enough. The pilot up in the air tells me that the runway might be a bit too short. I ask that that runway be extended, and I am told that there is no money available. It would cost less to extend the landing strip in Rouyn then it would to make the repeated stops at Val d'Or, Rouyn, Montreal, Val d'Or,

*
Rouyn, and Montreal. That is the kind of economy practised by Crown corporations.
Quebecair serves Val d'Or and that company makes money. Air Canada and the CNR make deficits. They are asked to improve their service in our areas. The CNR complains that people no longer use its trains to go to Quebec City or Montreal. Mr. Speaker, let them come with me on the CNR in the North and it is clear that they would not do it again. Only one trip would suffice. In fact, the service is not improving. There is the whole staff, all the employees who are travelling from Noranda to either Quebec City or Montreal. The train is divided first in Senneterre, and then in Hervey-Junction. One part of the train proceeds towards Montreal, while the other goes to Quebec City. The cars are almost empty, except for lumberjacks in the Clova area, but there are hardly any at all now.
Still, there is the transport of wood supplies towards either Montreal or Quebec City. Mr. Speaker, if the passenger service were better, the CNR would operate at a profit in these areas.
As for freight, the CN operates at profit. This is perhaps one of the most profitable activities of this Crown corporation in the field of lumber or mineral ore transportation from the North West. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is not aware of that and neither is the Canadian Transport Commission. And that Crown corporation, the CN, does not realize the possibilities-in that area, especially with the James Bay development which will last for more than 3 years. It may be a matter of 15, 20 or 25 years considering the new mines which will be discovered in that area. The CN might do well to get off the pot and ensure that their services improve rather than content themselves with asking for votes-to pay their good-for-nothing people or make up for their deficits due to poor management. To ask that votes be passed to improve services would be more encouraging.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that these Crown corporations should not be used to compete unfairly with private trucking enterprise, which is a viable and a worthwhile industry. Because it is that, it is made to compete against an unfair rival which depends on moneys voted by Parliament.
Every year, the same thing happens. I have been here for 15 years and every year we are asked to make up the CNR and Air Canada deficits yet we hear my socialist friends attack the Canadian Pacific and CP Air because these two concerns are making profits.
Private enterprise carries on a profitable business while the Crown corporation registers deficits. And yet, we are not convinced. Rather than say: Let us improve the Canadian National services, we say: Nationalize the Canadian Pacific to make it like the Canadian National.
For our part, we say: Either abandon the Canadian National or force it to continue its operations in the same manner as the Canadian Pacific. Then, we shall have fewer budget allowances to vote and we shall not have to support the insatiable spenders that government corporations are.
Mr. Speaker, enough is enough and I sincerely believe that there are abuses as concerns the expenditures of
October 18, 1973

government corporations such as Air Canada and the Canadian National. I think that the time has come for the government to accept its responsibilities and protect private initiative and enterprise in Canada.
It is not by giving billions of dollars to deficit ridden corporations that we shall promote the normal development of a country like ours. We often hear complaints such as those expressed a while ago by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan). He speaks of Newfoundland and says that it is a new Canadian province and that Newfoundland alone is different from other provinces. The same thing is said about other areas.
In western Manitoba and Quebec, you can hear the same complaints. Things will continue to go badly as long as we do not have a uniform policy for all Canada, including Newfoundland and British Columbia, and as long as we do not realize that when you step on the tail of the dog owned by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate, the same dog barks in Vancouver.
Do you understand? This means an equal and uniform policy, one that is beneficial to all Canadians, and that is what the Creditists wish with all their hearts for Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very happy to hear the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) indicate to this House that men were leaving the CNR to work for private truckers because private truckers manage their businesses well, as private enterprise can, and provide better working conditions and pay. I hope this indicates that the the NDP are finally seeing the light and realize that some of the management techniques of public ownership are not very good and the working people of this country would be far better off if they did not have to put up with some of the things that happen in the public management of business. I was also happy to hear the hon. member for Fraser Valley West talk about American control of unions and control of pension funds, and to hear him criticize the unions. That was a refreshing theme to hear from the NDP who so often seem to be under the thumb of the unions. In our debate of just a month ago in settling the railway dispute, that party did everything possible to prevent the settlement of the dispute by voting against the bill and against the amendments produced by this party.
To give some further information and light with respect to the pension fund held by the CNR, I want to tell the House that in the financial statement of the Canadian National Railways the total amount of reserves in the pension fund as of December 31, 1972, was $1,454 million, a considerably larger amount than indicated by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West. Further concerning pensions, I note that in 1971, while $261,800,000 was put into the pension fund only $75 million was paid out to workmen who are retired or have otherwise left the CNR. Clearly, the pension fund is growing like a monster, and clearly retired workmen are entitled to something better. I hope the investigation by John Deutsch will show that this kind of money should not lie dead and that men who contribute should get a decent pension.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
This bill, which is of a similar nature to those produced by ministers of finance in the past, permits more money to come from the public till to Canadian National Railways and to Air Canada. In analysing the need for money, I think it is high time we said something about what appears in the balance sheets of the CNR and Air Canada. For a moment I would like to deal with those balance sheets and put on record some of the financial facts as they really are. They are pretty hard to find in the balance sheets, but let us see what we can do.
Before I do that, however, I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that when I was a young fellow going to high school and eventually to university, they kept telling me it was no wonder the CNR kept losing money. After all, it had to take over all these bankrupt railway lines, bail out these foreign capitalists and take over all this property that wasn't worth a darn. They had to run horrid transportation lines through uneconomic areas, through towns that were not "making it," and areas that were no good for agriculture, mining or anything else. My investigations show that that is not so.
We all have had something to do with real estate. Just look around at some of the real estate held by the CNR, real estate in downtown Toronto, not cheap real estate but about the most expensive you can possibly buy. Mr. Speaker, the debt of the CNR is more than covered, many times more than paid off in the inflated values given to the CNR in the enormous properties they hold in every city in Canada in downtown locations. There is absolutely no reason, if those assets were used properly, why the corporation should have any debt at all.
Let us get into the debt factor. From the CNR's financial statement we find that the corporation has gross assets with a book value-remember, the land we are talking about did not cost a dollar in many cases and the rights of way were given them free; a great amount of the property they have is totally depreciated and was written off long ago-of $4.2 billion and it owes approximately $1.9 billion. You can say that that is a lot of debt. It is a lot of debt. But of that $1.9 billion, $1.1 billion is owed to the government of Canada and much of it on terms that bear no interest whatsoever. So when we talk about the real debt of the CNR, it is about $800 million and the highest interest rate paid on that debt to the public market-that is the only real debt there is, the public market debt-is 534 per cent per annum. Any other debt of the CNR, if interest is paid on it at all, is paid into the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, as I say, at rates that bear no relevance to the cost of money. Having analysed that, we find that the interest paid on this $1.9 billion debt was only $66 million.
Let us go on to the next question. Look at the revenue of this national railway. I am rounding the figures off because there is no point in filling Hansard with long, detailed figures. We find from the financial statement that the CNR took in gross revenue, from its operations last year, $1.4 billion. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), the debt charges, compared with the gross income of the corporation, for the year ending December 31, 1972, were 2.1 per cent of the gross revenues. Any corporation can certainly afford to carry that small debt factor.

October 18, 1973
Capital Punishment
But what does the CNR do? What do these directors do with their fancy annual balance? They produce a table and show that if they did not have to pay any interest, they would make a profit. And what interest do they have to pay? They pay $66 million in interest, and they say that is why they lost $17 million. They did $1.4 billion worth of business. Their debt and their interest costs represent only 2.1 per cent of their total revenues, and they cook their balance sheet to show that that crushing debt is hurting them.
When analysing the situation, Mr. Speaker, I think we should look at the balance sheet of that other railroad in Canada which for some strange reason always makes a very good profit. I went to the library and got the balance sheet of the CPR for the year ending December 31, 1972, and found that it had a gross revenue in that year of $709 million-half the gross revenue of the CNR-and it had a debt of $267 million on which it paid interest of roughly $25 million. The debt ratio to the gross business done by the CPR was not 2.1 per cent of the gross but 2.8 per cent. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the CPR did not complain about the fact that it had to pay interest. It showed a profit. The cost of money borrowed by the CPR was 2.8 per cent of the gross revenue, but the cost of money borrowed by the CNR was 2.1 per cent of its gross revenue. That clearly indicates to me, as it should to every member of this House, that it is not the debt that causes the problem in the CNR but is, perhaps, inept management. The CPR, paying a greater share of its gross revenue to service the interest on its funded debt, makes a profit; and the CNR, which ever since I can remember has been screaming about the horrid cost of its debt, has only 2.1 per cent of its gross revenue going to service its debt.
In making this interesting comparison between the private railroad and the public railroad regarding profit and revenues and other business aspects, I found it is very difficult to discover the right figures because of the way the companies set up their balance sheets. Some adding and subtracting is necessary. Consolidated balance sheets of corporations reflect the consolidation of a number of operations, and consequently one has to realize that what is treated as one item in one balance sheet may not be the same item in the next balance sheet. As I mentioned, Mr. Speaker, at the last year-end Canadian Pacific Railway had done $709 million worth of business.
